Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to direct the attention of the First Alinister to a practice which seems to obtain a good deal this session, that of moving the House into Supply two or three hours after dinner, when neither the Prime Minister nor any of the other ministers are in their places. In the days of my parliamentary innocence it was the practice, I think, to move the House into Supply when the Prime Minister and most of his colleagues were here, and I would like to see that practice resumed. It may be fastidious on my part to vent this idea, but I would like to see it observed a little more, so that the undoubted right of every member of parliament to discuss some public question on going into Supply may be maintained, and that the ministers may be in their places to hear what is said.
I understand that the only time when the House was moved into Committee of Supply at a later hour than eight o'clock was yesterday.
No ; two or three times.

speechtext: I understand the contrary. At all events, the House can always be moved into Committee of Supply to oblige my hon. friend or any other hon. member who wants to make a motion. Of course, the House may be moved into Committee of Supply at any moment; but we have usually taken up Bills before going into Committee of Supply. Of course, if I knew in advance that any hon. gentleman wished to bring up any question on the motion to go into Committee of Supply, I would be only too glad to give him the opportunity.

Hon. RAYMOND PREFONTAINE (Minister of Alarine and Fisheries) moved second reading of Bill (No. 37) to amend the Quebec Harbour Commissioners Act, 1899. He said :	The object is to extend about
three miles further down the River St. Lawrence the pilotage limits of the Quebec

district. At present steamers have to ,stop at Father Point to get the mails and then they have to stop at Bie, 17 miles farther up in order to take on pilots. It is recommended by those interested in shipping that the pilotage limit be extended to Father Point and the pilots be taken on board there and thus avoid the necessity of a second stoppage.
Have all the shipping interests asked for that ?
Every one.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and House went into committee on the Bill.
On section 1,
What is the object of extending the jurisdiction of the Harbour Commissioners ?

The limits are now 17 miles above Father Point and steamers are obliged to stop at Bic to take on pilots. They are also obliged to stop at Father Point, about 17 miles further down, to take the mails, but if the limits be extended to Father Point, the pilots can be taken on board there as well as the mail and thus only one stoppage will be necessary.
Is this the only Bill to be introduced by the government this session to amend the Quebec Harbour Commissioner's Act ?
I am not aware of any other nor of any demands for any other change.
Is there anything in the law which compels the pilots to be taken on at Bic ?

The pilots of the Port of Quebec are under the jurisdiction of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners and the pilots are taken on at the extreme eastern limit of the pilotage district. The shipping federations have represented time and again that this should be remedied, and the pilots taken on at Father Point as well as the mails. But unless we extend the limits of the pilotage district, we cannot oblige a pilot to go down to Father Point, because outside the pilotage district he is outside the authority of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners.
I thought that the hon. minister last session intended to bring in a Bill to take the control of pilotage into the hands of the Dominion government.

The pilotage authority for the district of Montreal, extending from Montreal to Quebec was given to the Department of Marine and Fisheries last year with the consent of all public bodies interested. But as regards the Que-

bee district, no one would consent to this change. Even the Shipping Federation and others specially interested would not consent. I am informed however, though not officially, that they will make a request in the course of the next week that the pilotage authority for the district of Quebec be put into the bands of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. But I have not yet received any official demand.
Is the reason the hon. minister gives the only one for changing the law ?
Yes.
What about steamers such as the ' Gampana ' which go to the maritime provinces ?
They have no pilots.	.
They are not under the jurisdiction of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners ?

No. I wish to propose an amendment to subsection B of this section by adding at the end of the words ' the river Saguenay excepted.' Through an error in preparing the Bill these words were not inserted, and they should be there because the pilotage on the Saguenay was last year put under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

I take this opportunity of calling the attention of the House to a petition with regard to telephones. This petition, which has been signed by a large number of municipal corporations all over the country prays :
That your honourable House may be pleased to pass an Act amending all charters granted to telephone companies so as to declare that the poles of such companies shall not be hereafter erected or conduits constructed on any road or street in a municipality without the consent of the council of such municipality, and upon such terms as such council may approve.
As things are now', it would appear, a telephone company incorporated under a Dominion charter can override these municipal rights and can enter upon the streets of any municipality without askiiig the consent of the corporation. This has been found a very substantial grievance and parliament is being petitioned to remove it.
Is there a general statute, on the subject ?

There may be some general statute in regard to it, but, so far as I can see, it does not cover the case completely. When a delegation of representatives of leading municipalities waited upon the government, the Minister of Justice asked them to draft a clause which they would like to see put in the general law, at least that is the representation that has been made to me. The municipalities all over this country feel that their rights are being encroached upon by the wide powers taken by the telephone company. And another petition is in circulation, but whether presented to the House or not I do not know. It is a petition on behalf of the Union of Canadian Municipalities. They pray the Dominion government and parliament to carry out the following legislation :
1.	The purchase by the government of the long distance lines.
2.	The amendment of all existing telephone charters, so as to provide that no companies shall erect poles or construct conduits on any road or street in a municipality without the consent of the council of such municipality, and upon such terms as such council may approve.
Here are two organizations, the municipalities on their own account and the Union of Canadian Municipalities praying parliament to give them jurisdiction over the erection of poles or laying of conduits by telephone companies within their limits ; and I trust the government may be able this session to introduce a general law dealing with that question and restoring to the municipalities the full control of their own streets in these matters. It may be necessary to allow these companies to go through a municipality with their long-distance service, but I contend it never was the intention of parliament to take jurisdiction over the streets of municipalities and hand it over to telephone companies. But there is a still more important question involved. It is referred to in ' The Canadian Engineer' as follows :
With regard to the government ownership and control of the long distance lines, while we endorse any movement for the public ownership of utilities, we believe it is far more essential at the present time, for the government to call upon the Bell Telephone Company to give and receive connection over the long distance lines of its existing system with the subscribers of all local telephone services, without regard to the ownership of such exchanges. In other words, every telephone user should have the right of long distance service whether he is a Bell subscriber or not. The inevitable result' of this would be that the monopoly would no longer be able to keep out local competition, municipal and independent exchanges would be established in all parts of the Dominion, and in a few years the demand for increased long distance telephone facilities would be such that the government would be compelled to recognize the necessity of establishing a state-owned long distance system, either by duplicating or
acquiring and extending the lines of the Bell Telephone Company.
Now, tbat is tbe most important question in connection with tbe telephone service. This calls for an interchange of what I might call telephone traffic. The law of Canada concerning railways provides that railway companies must interchange traffic. But at present the Bell Telephone Company or any other, can refuse to give connection to an independent company. The consequence is that the Bell Telephone Company has a monopoly throughout the country. This matter came up in the railway committee the other day. When I proposed to put in a private Bill incorporating a telephone company a clause compelling the company to allow interchange of traffic, the hon. acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) who is chairman of that committee, said that this ought to be incorporated in a general measure. I agreed with him. But I went further and said that the government should assume the responsibility and introduce such a measure. In view of the petitions that have been presented, I take it to be the duty of the government, this session to make a general law compelling an interchange of traffic between the telephone companies. It is true that a telephone company to-day will accept a measure from i another company if carried across the road and handed into their office; but they will not do what railway companies are compelled to do, make connections so that the traffic can go from one line to the other. Every telephone company has been created by parliament and given powers of incorporation because it is declared to be in the public interest. That is the very basis of the reasons given for incorporating them-that they are in the general interest of Canada. That being the ease, the general interest of Canada can govern them as it governs the railway companies. And the government, out of respect for that interest, should ask parliament to pass a law to compel the telephone companies to interchange traffic. Let me put it as ' The Canadian Engineer ' puts it:
We would point out that the charter of the Bell Company declares the works of that corporation to be ' for the general advantage of Canada.' Th'at being so, the Bell Company has no more right to restrict the use of its long distance system to its own subscribers, than a railway company has to refuse to haul the cars of another system over its lines. We do not, of course, suggest that the company should not be compensated for the use of its lines by outside companies. A system similar to that in operation in Great Britain for the use of the government long distance lines could be arranged without difficulty. In Great Britain a subscriber to the Glasgow Municipal Telephone exchange wishing to speak to a subscriber of the National Telephone Company in London, Manchester, Liverpool or elsewhere, would pay.

I had it written.
iSir WILFRID LAURIER. I did not receive any notice, had I done so I would have been glad to place in his hands for his own information the report of an interview he referred to, and which took place some time ago with a deputation from the city of Toronto, if I remember right, with regard to some of the privileges which are now held by the Bell Telephone Company. So far as I remember, the grievance which was brought to our attention by the city deputation was in consequence of a decision given by the Judicial Committee of the .Privy Council whereby it was held that the Bell Telephone Company could use the streets of Toronto, and put poles in the streets ; they had not only the use of the streets which they had already been using, but of all the streets in the city. As I understand the charter given to the Bell Telephone Company in 1S82, they had not only the right to use certain streets, they were already using, but the power to go all over the city and cover its streets with their poles. If I remember the request which was made to us by the mayor and solicitor of the city of Toronto, it was that parliament should pass a law to abridge the power thus given by parliament to the Bell Telephone Company. Well, for my part I pointed out to the mayor and to the solicitor that in my judgment that would be interfering with rights which had been given by parliament. They thought it would not be an interference, but that a clause could be framed whereby the Act would be so amended as that it would not infringe upon the vested rights they had in the city. Thereupon we asked the solicitor and the mayor to frame an amendment for our consideration so that we might have in concrete form the very thing they wanted us to do, whether we would agree to it or not. So far, however, we have not received this draft legislation. If such draft legislation were received by us, it would be our duty to consider it and see whether we could introduce it to this House. I would say to my hon. friend at once that if such an amendment could be framed, one which would not interfere with any vested rights of the Bell Telephone Company, I can see no objection why such a law should not be introduced. But if such a law cannot be introduced without infringing upon rights which have been granted to the company by this parliament, there would be a serious objection to such legislation. I pass no judgment at this moment upon the question which has been raised. I have been waiting, and am still waiting, for news from the city of Toronto upon this subject.
This brings me to another point which has been mentioned by my hon. friend. He has asked for a good deal of legislation, and 40
one of the things he is asking for is a restoration to the municipalities of the powers which have been invaded by this parliament. I am not aware that parliament has ever, by any general law, invaded the powers of municipalities. But I am aware that in past legislation, private companies, the Bell Telephone Company for instance, have been allowed to invade municipalities^ to invade Toronto and other cities, without any reference to municipal authority. Last year, or the year before, our attention was called to similar legislation which was asked for by some railway corporation; and, if I remember right, the Railway Committee here would not pass any law which would interfere with the powers of any municipality unless the consent of the municipality had first been obtained. I am pretty sure that at this moment the tendency and desire of the House would be at all times to see that the rights and privileges of the municipalities are not interfered with except witli their consent. I do not know whether there will be any necessity of passing a law with this object in view. But, in regard to another matter which has been brought up by my hon. friend I confess that I, to a large extent, sympathize with him when he says that the time has come when we should have some general law regulating telephonic traffic and the interchange of traffic between telephone lines. For my part I think there is great force in the demand which has been made in this House and which has been presented to us in numerous petitions. This is a matter which ought to engage the attention of the House, but before it engages the attention of the House it ought to engage the attention of the government. I do not say what will be the course of the government this session or at any future session; all I can say is that the government is not at all oblivious to the sentiment which prevails in the country and I think some attention ought to be given to the question.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad that the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has brought the attention of the House to this matter. I think I can supply some information from my own county upon this subject which is only an illustration of the general condition of affairs as far as private telephone companies are concerned. There have been two private companies established in my county for the last four or five years, and their purpose is to give the people living in the back townships telephonic connection with the railways. One of them especially has its terminus at a station of the Canadian Pacific Railway, an important distributing centre of trade, but by virtue of an agreement entered into between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Bell Telephone Company the Canadian Pacific Railway refuses to permit that private telephone company to place a tele-



phone box in the station. The result is that nine-tenths of the clients of the Canadian Pacific Railway at that station cannot have telephonic communication with the station through which they receive all their freight and goods. They are obliged to send their messages to the telephone office in the village and then pay a special rate for a messenger to go down the hill 400 or 500 yards to deliver them to the agent at the station. They cannot communicate directly with the agent; they can only send a messenger. And, mind you, there is no office of the Bell Telephone Company there, but simply by virtue of the monopoly they enjoy that private telephone company are not permitted to place a box in the office of the Canadian Pacific Railway notwithstanding the fact that the Bell Telephone Company have no office there. The Bell Telephone Company have no office there or at the village, but they exercise their right of monopoly even where they have no, traffic at all. As far as the principle of vested rights is concerned in theory I quite agree with my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), but we must not forget this that when rights were grantej for the Bell Telephone Company telephonic traffic was not then considered such as it is now a matter of general interest to the whole country. We had not then come to the point of seeing that the telephone system that does not belong to the companies who enjoy its profits but that it belongs to the people at large, and the time must come when vested rights which were at one time considered to be private property cannot longer be allowed to interfere with the rights of the public. The rights of the public must be considered and if the rights of a private company interfere with the rights of the people then parliament should rather side with the public interest than with private interest. But, it should be done with a great deal of care. We should not introduce that principle with the Idea that in consideration of the public interest we should entirely disregard vested rights, but at the same time I think the government should look into the question. I hope they are going to look into it very soon and that they will not be entirely biased by the idea of protecting vested rights. They should consider vested rights, but if there is a conflict between public and private rights, public rights should have the preference over private rights.

Mr. Speaker, with a great deal of what the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said I would agree, but there is one thing with which I would not agree, that is that it is only the duty of the government to take up grievances when some one has brought in a Bill to remedy them. I have always regarded it as the duty of the government to recognize a grievance when it is brought to their notice in various ways and then to Mr. BOURASSA.
endeavour to find a remedy. This grievance has been brought to the attention of the government over and over again, for several years past and I respectfully submit that it should not be left to a private member to bring in a Bill to remedy it. The condition existing in his locality so graphically described by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) is what may be found all over this country and it has been brought to the attention of the government over and over again. If I understand it correctly a railway company, when it receives its charter, agrees, by virtue of that charter, to give to the public alike equal facilities to do business with the company. Can it be said that a railway company is carrying out that agreement if it deprives the people who live in one section of the country of the right to do business over the telephone line with its station while it gives that right to another class of people ?

The case I have cited is still worse than that. The Bell Telephone Company has no office there but it prevents the private company which is the only one that has a line there from having connection with the station.

Yes, but I was dealing with this question. It is absolutely the duty of the railway company to deal with all people who use that railway upon the same principle and to give them equal facilities. It cannot be successfully contended that a railway company is giving equal facilities to people who live alongside a private line when it denies them the right of connecting their line with the station while at the same time it gives people living upon the line of the Bell Telephone Company the right to do business with the station. I am anxious to get the ear of the right hon. Prime Minister, but if I am only talking to deaf ears I would rather avoid the trouble of talking at all. I do not say anything about the discourtesy that is displayed to a member of the House who is endeavouring to do his duty because I think every hon. minister ought to recognize that which is fairly due to another member. I say in regard to this question that in my judgment the duty of the government is, now that the grievance is brought to their attention, to provide a law to remedy and not call upon private members to perform that duty. This case has been brought to their attention over and over again. Then, another feature of this matter is that I hold that the law as it is to-oay would compel the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other railway to admit any other telephone company to its office if the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) took the matter up and enforced the law. You cannot expect a private individual will undertake to fight against a railway company. This has become such an intolerable grievance to business people that the government ought to take it up and remedy it at the earliest

possible date. When we endeavour in every Bill that comes before the House and the Railway Committee to embody in it a clause providing a remedy for this grievance we are invariably met by some member of the government with the objection that this remedy should be provided by a general Act. Well, let the government introduce that Act and pass it. We will give them all the support we can and I am sure the people are desirous that it should be done. I think the government are not doing their duty by the people if they do not provide a remedy when the grievance is brought to their attention.
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter in which I am very much interested.

speechtext: There is no motion before the House. If there is to be a long discussion-
I understood that a motion had been made to go into Supply and it was to that motion that I addressed myself.

This is a matter of very great moment to the country. Some time ago I placed certain questions with regard to it upon the order paper and requested an answer with regard to a particular instance, namely, the difficulty with the Bell Tele-pliom Company which was brought to the attention of the government during the last session in reference to making connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway offices at Port Arthur and Fort William. I was told. I think, by the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Emmerson), that it was impossible to answer these questions although they were put in succinct and concrete form. For what reason he was unable to answer these questions and give the information I am unable at present to say. I regret to note that the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Conmee) is not in his place at this time. If he were here he could doubtless speak of the very great confusion that was caused to the commercial interests of Port Arthur and Fort William by this difficulty. There is in these towns the Bell Telephone system and also a municipal system. The Bell Company, armed with this public franchise granted to them by parliament and enjoying the public rights, and opportunities so granted absolutely, refused to make any connection whatever with the municipal telephone system or with the offices of the Canadian Pacific Railway, so that it was impossible for subscribers of the municipal system of Port Arthur and Fort William to have any telephone access to, or any communication with the railway stations at Port Arthur and Fort William, which were under the control of the Bell Telephone Company. A very large percentage of the people of these two towns which are large growing and prosperous towns of considerable and growing commercial im-40J
portanee, use the service of the Citizen Telephone Company. They prefer to use the Citizen's Company and to exercise the privilege which they have of patronizing their local municipal telephone system, but of what use was it to them when the Bell Company, enjoying these privileges granted to them, as the right hon. the Prime Minister says, by parliament, could set at naught the will of the peopljj and prevent them from having access to these offices and to the full use and enjoyment of their franchise. It is an important question and one that should occupy the attention of the government even at this late day. It is very much to be regretted indeed that the government has not, after all these grievances have been brought to its attention, seen fit to interfere, to remedy these grievances and bring before parliament some measure which would afford some relief under the circum-. stances.

Before the motion is adopted I would like to refer to the correspondence which the Prime Minister has just placed on the table. As it is not very long I shall take the opportunity of reading it. The first telegram is as follows :
Ottawa, 5th Oct., 1904.
Joseph Ena Girouard,
Dawson, Y.T.
You have been appointed returning officer for the electoral district of the Yukon. Writ dated 29th September mailed to-day. Nomination Friday, 18th November, at Dawson. With this information by referring to form ' E ' and clauses of Yukon Representation Act, 1902, you can select clerk and enumerator and decide on polling stations. Then prepare proclamation following directions in Act.
(Sgd.) R. W. SCOTT.
A note follows this :
On ascertaining that Girouard was a member of the Yukon Council and therefore disqualified, Ledieu was appointed.

Ottawa, 8th October, 1904.
Pierre Ledieu,
Barrister, Dawson, Yukon Territory.
You have been appointed returning officer in place of Joseph Ena Girouard, not' qualified. Get from him my telegram, October 5th, and act in accordance therewith.

The next telegram reads :
Ottawa, 17th October, 1904.
Pierre Ledieu,
Returning Officer, Dawson, Yukon.
If proclamation has not been posted slay action. Represented that owing to difficulty of travelling time appointed for nomination is unsuitable. Number of polling places should not exceed forty. Consult Congdon, who is familiar
with centres of population. Advise me immediately of present position.

Then there is a note following that to this effect:
Not then known that Congdon had resigned commissionership or that he was to be a candidate.
(Sgd.) R. W. S.
The next telegram is dated Dawson, Yukon, October 20, 1904:

Scott,
Secretary of State, Ottawa.
Is writ to be dated 5th October, and what is the return day ?
(Sgd.) PIERRE LEDIEU,
Returning Officer.
The next telegram is dated Ottawa, October 21, 1904, and is as follows :
Ottawa, 21 October, 1904.
Pierre Ledieu,
Dawson, Yukon Territory.
No, writ dated 29th September

nomination 18th November. You were instructed to get my telegram to Mr. Girouard and act in accordance with it. I cancel the suggestion in my telegram to stay action and expect you to proceed vigorously. If not too late limit number of polls to forty. Writ' returnable when your duties have been completed.

The next telegram is dated Dawson, Yukon Territory, and is dated December 5, 1904. It is to the Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick (Minister of Justice), and reads:
The voters' lists compiled.
I suppose it is compiled, it reads ' complied : '
The voters' lists compiled under the Yukon Territory Representation Act, 1902, have been stolen, if posted, immediately after posted ; lists for each polling division have not been posted in accordance with section 30, and access to lists in enumerators' hands under section 30 and 31 refused by enumerators to Dr. Alfred Thompson, candidate, his agents and supporting electors. Intense excitement prevails in consequence, pointing to danger of general uprising. The lists for whole enumeration district were posted in two places only in such district and were not segregated for polling subdivisions and posted in such polling divisions. Such lists as posted were so posted secretly at midnight, November 30th, and immediately removed and have never been open to be seen by Dr. Thompson or his supporters. We respectfully request that direct' instructions be immediately given to all enumerators to allow Dr. Thompson, his agents and all electors access to voters' lists, final closing of the same under Act. Please advise Dr. Thompson by wire.
(Sgd.) ALFRED THOMPSON.
'Candidate T. W. O'Brien, Thomas J. Kearney, N. F. Hagel, T. D. Patullo, C. W. Tobors, George Black, John Pringle, R. H. S. Cress-well, committee.
The next telegram is dated Ottawa, December 1, 1904 :

Ottawa, 7 December, 1904.
Pierre Ledieu,
Returning Officer, Dawson, Y.T.
All candidates are entitled to equal facilities in securing copies voters' lists. Representations are being made that this rule is not being *observed. Any sharp or indefensible practice defeating this fair principle by officers employed under Elections Act will result in forfeiture of their remuneration and may void the election. You appointed clerks and enumerators and will be held responsible for any malfeasance. Publish this telegram immediately on receipt in local papers and send me copy of papers. Answer by wire if published.

It appears by tlie subsequent correspondence that the returning officer did not obey the very proper instructions which the Secretary of State gave to him by publishing this telegram ; in fact further on he intimates that he has declined or refused to obey these instructions so far as the publication is concerned. The telegram which follows next is :
Dawson, Y.T., Dec. 7, 1904. Secretary State, Scott,
Ottawa.
Returning officer Pierre Ledieu refuses to make public through newspapers contents or purport of instructions known to have been received from you. People vitally interested. Please wire ' News ' if the public is entitled to know.
Dawson ' Daily News,'
A. S. GEORGE, editor.
To this the following reply was sent:
Quebec, 9 Dec., 1904.
A. S. George, editor, &c.,
Dawson, Y. T.
Returning officer was substantially instructed to give all candidates equal opportunities to obtain copies of voters' lists. That as he had appointed enumerators it was in his power to see that the lists were given impartially to both candidates.

The next telegram is from the Yukon to the Secretary of State.
Dawson, Y.T., Dec. 9, 1904.

Scott,
Halifax, N.S.
List as yet not furnished Dr. Thompson or his agent. Returning officer neglects to communicate with enumerators outside Dawson and some enumerators are being kept hidden. He refuses list of polling subdivisions until two days before election, too late for electors to ascertain whether names on are struck off. Other party has them. People depending on you but thoroughly aroused, have had to request police to protect enumerators and returning officer to-day. If corroboration desired communicate with Police Commissioner Wood. Instructions should be prompt and definite, and Dr. Thompson advised thereof, otherwise same will be evaded. Situation becoming more strained.
ALFRED THOMPSON, candidate, John Pringle, T. W. O'Brien, Thos. J. Kearney, C. W. Clabor, N. W. Hagel, George Black, R. H. S. Cresswell, T D. Patullo.

The next telegram is from the returning officer:
Dawson, Y.T., Dec. 9th, 1904. Hon. R. W. Scott,
Halifax, N.S.
I repudiate any intimation that I have facilitated one candidate more than the other in obtaining special copies of voters' lists. The law as framed does not provide for furnishing such special copies to each candidate by enumerators, whose only duty is to post the same in the different divisions. True it is that several of them were stolen after being posted. Each partv accuses the other of the theft. I remain uncertain as to what was my duty, but will follow your instructions by advising the enumerators to furnish each candidate with special [DOT]copies. The duties of returning officers under the Yukon Representation Act are not clear. 1 thank you for your opinion upon the matter, i beg however, to submit that the publication ot your telegram would be unjust towards me by putting me in an unfair light before the public. I hope you will not insist upon the execution of this order. 1 cannot understand how your telegram was known to have been sent before it
reached me.	pieRRE DEDIEU,
Returning Officer.
Ottawa, 31st' Jan., 1905.
Pierre Ledieu,
Returning Officer, Dawson, Y.T.
Whom do you propose declaring as member elect ? Reports received give Thompson a large majority.
R. W. SCOTT. Dawson, Y.T., Feb. 1, 1905.
R. W. Scott,
Ottawa, Ont.
I propose, as bound by law, to declare elected the candidate who on the 7th February, declaration day, will be found to have had the majority of votes. As it Is I have only the unofficial reports of deputy returning officers, which apparently give a majority to Thompson of over 500.

Returning Officer.
Dawson, Y.T., Feb. 8, 1905.

Secretary State, Ottawa.

Returning Officer.
The telegram of the Secretary of State reflected in no wise on the returning officer. It was a mere telegram of instructions, and it does credit to the Secretary of State in that regard. It is evident from the telegram which I have just read that it was not the intention of the returning officer to comply with those instructions, but to keep secret from the public until after the election the instructions which he had thus received. And I may say, before I go on to the further telegrams, that this returning officer points out what we pointed out to the government during the last session and the session before that if the law were not amended grave injustice would be done to candidates where there were partisan returning officers or enumerators, both in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon. The very thing which we pointed out, which my friend Mr. Casgrain, who then represented Montmorency, predicted, in his address to the House on that occasion, has actually happened in the Yukon and has led to serious disturbances there. I thought it worth while to read this correspondence to the House, because it deals with a very important matter, namely, the conduct of the returning officer, who is an officer of this House ; and it concerns also the disfranchisement of the Yukon Territory for a period of perhaps two months when it should have been represented by its member sitting in this House. When this matter was mentioned earlier in the session, my lion, friend the Minister of Justice stated distinctly that an explanation was to he demanded from the returning officer as to the reason for delaying the date for opening the ballot boxes and summing up the result, to the 7th day of February, the necessity for which does not appear anywhere in this correspondence, nor, so far as I am aware, can it be demonstrated otherwise. The promise then made to the House by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice has apparently, for some reason, been overlooked or neglected.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to say that I do not know much of the circumstances which have attended this election. In fact, I knew nothing of them until a day or two ago, when, after my hon. friend the leader of the opposition had brought the matter to the attention of the House, I made some inquiry as to the reason for the delay in returning the elected member. All the information that I can give at this moment to my hon. friend is this, that according to the law and the practice of the Yukon, the delay has not been extraordinary. If I am correctly informed, there must be according to the law of the Yukon a full month between nomination day and polling day, and a very long delay between polling day and declaration day. The reason is that at that season especially, on account of the long distances and the severity of the weather and the bad roads, it would not be possible to have any less delay. If I am correctly informed, the returning officer on this occasion acted exactly in accordance with the precedent of the previous election in the Yukon. There have been two elections in the Yukon so far, first, the election of Mr. Ross and then the election of Dr. Thompson. As I am informed, the delays in each were exactly the same, and those delays had been fixed by the returning officer before the two candidates were put in nomi nation. The impression seems to prevail that they were extended by the present returning officer after the election of Dr. Thompson, because Dr. Thompson was supposed not to be of his own political party ; but if I am correctly informed, all such imputations are absolutely unfounded. The delays were exactly the same as before and were fixed at the time the returning officer issued his proclamation fixing the polling days and the day for declaration. As my hon. friend has read, the last telegram sent by the Secretary of State to the returning officer was that he should declare elected the candidate having the majority and that his duty was to send his return here, and as soon as we have his return we will be in a position to see how the matter stands.

There was no delay so far as the former member of the Yukon is concerned, but that may have been due to the fact that the House met at a later date in the year. But I would be slow to be-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
lieve, without very cogent evidence, that a delay of fifty-three days is necessary for the return of the ballot boxes. That is the delay which has taken place in this instance from the 16th December until the 7th February.

I notice in the public prints, within the last day or two, copies of orders which the Militia Council proposes to put in force regarding those clerks in the Militia Department who are in the militia of Canada. I wish to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Militia to one of the clauses in these orders. It is a clause which, it seems to me, cannot fail to create a wrong impression, and an impression which, I feel sure, the hon. minister had no intention of producing. The clause says that-	' .

similar considerations govern the grant of leave of absence for the purpose of attending annual training or performing other military duty. Leave of absence, other than the annual leave to which the applicant is entitled under the Civil Service Act, can only be given for this purpose upon the condition that no detriment is caused to the public service.
That is the clause to which I call attention. We all know well that no employer in this country can have any of his men belong to the militia without suffering some detriment to his business. This clause refers to times of peace, and the other parts of the order, which refer to times of war, provide that the members of the civil service in the Militia Department shall not go out in time of war. That is probably all right. But in times of peace, I feel quite certain that even if these orders are put in force as they read, the minister will never prevent any of the clerks in his department from going to annual drill, simply because that might cause the department some inconvenience. I am sure that the hon, minister wishes to make the militia as efficient as possible, and I simply wish to suggest that the clause to which I have referred, and which provides that the clerks in the Militia Department cannot attend annual drill in time of peace if it causes any detriment to the public service, is one which will produce an impression among other employers of labour that will do our militia a lot of harm. No employer of labour can allow his men to belong to the militia without some detriment to his business ; and I am quite sure that the Minister of Militia is willing that his department should, in time of peace, be put to the ordinary inconvenience or detriment which other people are willing to suffer when their men belong to the force. I would suggest that before these orders are put in force the hon. minister should consider whether he should not alter the wording of this clause in order to remove from the minds of ordinary em-

ployers of labour the impression that the Department of Militia is not willing to be put to any detriment or inconvenience in order to allow its clerks to attend annual drill and the other ordinary duties of militiamen in times of peaee.

I am sorry I was not in the House when the motion was made, and still more that my hon. friend did not Intimate to me that he intended to bring this matter up. That is the usual course pursued and the usual courtesy extended to a minister. 1 was near the chamber in my own room attending to some work, and would have been here if I had known the intention of my hon. friend. Besides it would have been much more convenient to give the minister the opportunity of being prepared to meet a matter of this kind. Speaking off-hand, I may say that the reason for the order is that it would be manifestly inconvenient, in time of stress, or difficulty, or war, if you like, for officers of the Militia Department, who, at such a time, are more required in their offices than at any other, to be compelled to go into the field. It would be absolutely impossible to carry on important militia work if men holding important positions in the department were permitted to take posts in the militia which would necessitate their leaving their duties in the department at the very moment when they were most needed there, and when they could do best service for their country in the department itself. That is the whole object of the order. It was discussed in the Militia Council, and very strongly recommended by the four military experts, and was not passed without being most carefully considered. With all deference to my hon. friend, I do think that these gentlemen, possibly, are better informed than he as to the best requirements in the puhlic interest on the part of these officials in the Militia Department ; and I am sure that no one can have a stronger desire than they to serve the public interest. Later on, perhaps, in the session I shall be very glad to return to a discussion of this matter, but I think that this is rather an inopportune moment to consider it.

It is my purpose to take this matter up on the minister's estimates. No doubt the theory is that these men are all members of a permanent corps, so to speak, and to take them from one branch of the service to another in time of stress might be detrimental to the public interest. The point I specially object to is that it names certain commissions that no officer in the department may hold, such as adjutant, and, I believe, commanding officer. If an official is allowed to enlist as a private in a militia corps, I do not see why he should not 'be allowed to rise to be Lieutenant-Colonel of his regiment. Either these officials should not be allowed to join a militia corps or they should be free to rise
to the highest positions in the new service they are capable of taking. I give the minister intimation that I will take up this matter when the estimates are under consideration.

I think it would be well to have this order placed upon ' Hansard,' and therefore with the permission of the House, I will read it:
The question of to what extent it is desirable that employees of the Department of Militia and Defence, both at headquarters and elsewhere, should serve in the militia has been under the consideration of the minister in Militia Council.
It is obvious that in the event of an outbreak of war, the position of the Department of Militia and Defence must be entirely different from that of other departments of the public service. Upon its efficient working depends the efficiency of the military forces in the field. It is. therefore, of paramount importance for the success of the campaign that it should not suffer detriment by being liable to have members of its civil staff withdrawn at such a moment in order to serve with troops in the field.
At the same time, the Minister in Council desires to encourage employees of the department to serve in time of peace and so familiarize themselves with military requirements.
He trusts, however, that they will understand that, although they are members of the militia force of Canada, their duty to the State is primarily that of civil servants in the department to which they belong, and that in time of emergency they render more valuable service to their country by continuing to serve in the Militia Department than by accompanying their units as soldiers.
This being the ease, it follows that no employee of the Militia Department can be safely reckoned on to accompany his militia unit when it is called out for service, and further, that he ought not to hold any position in that unit of such a nature that his absence would seriously prejudice its military efficiency.
The Minister in Council has, therefore, decided that no civil employee of the Militia Department shall, in future, accept the position of either adjutant or commanding officer of any unit of the active militia, and that permission to join any corps can only be granted subject to this proviso.
Similar considerations govern the grant of leave of absence for the purpose of attending annual training or performing other military duty. Leave of absence, other than the annual leave to which the applicant is entitled under the Civil Service Act, can only be given for this purpose upon the condition that no detriment is caused to the public service.
All officers and other persons in the employment of the department will guide themselves accordingly.
