Railways and Canals-chargeable to capital- Welland canal-to deepen portions of summit level between Port Colborne and Thorold, $80,000.

As I explained last evening, $140,000 is required to complete tills work. We ask here for $80,000, wliicb will cover the work that, in the ordinary course, will he done within the fiscal year which will leave a balance of $60,000 to be asked for later on.
Last year $150,000 was voted for this purpose, which, with the $140,000 yet to be spent would make a total of $290,000.
The total estimated cost of this work is $530,000, of which $390,000 has been expended up to December 31 last.
Will this $140,000 complete the work ?
Yes, so I am informed by the chief engineer. The work is the excavation of 1,377,000 cubic yards. The lowest tender was 38i cents, making $530,000.
What depth of water will there be when the work is finished ?

This will give 17 feet of water at the ordinary level of Lake Erie, and 15 feet at low water. The deepening of the canal is made necessary by reason of the lowering of the water in Lake Erie which lias been going on for some years.
What is the object of having 17 feet when navigation in the canal is only 14 feet ?
When this is completed there will be a depth of 17 feet. At certain points the boats dragged, I believe making the deepening of this level necessary.
Why have 17 feet when you have only 14 feet of navigation ?

I have some knowledge of the navigation of the Welland canal. The difficulty arises from the fact that the wind blowing from the east to the west lowers the water in the Welland canal. When the wind is blowing from the west the water in the canal will rise two feet or more ; and when it is blowing from the east up the lake the water in the canal will be lowered by two feet or more. The normal depth of the water is supposed to be 14 feet, that is the advertised depth of water in the Welland canal, the depth on the mitre sill. There being this fluctuation of two feet above or below, it is necessary that the canal from Port Colborne to Thorold. where the locks begin, should have a sufficient depth of water so that when the wind is blowing up you will still have 14
feet. Unless that is done the canal at certain times would be absolutely useless.

When it was first built it was well known what the effect of the wind was, blowing east or west on Lake Erie. The difference between the two extreme levels was, I think, about six feet. There would be no object in deepening the summit level if you have not dropped the mitre sills both on the lake and at the entrance. Have you done that ?
Yes, at Port Colborne.

How much ?
Mr. EMMERaON. Three feet.

Then you are deepening the summit level of the canal for the purpose of bringing it down to the depth on the mitre sill, and at the entrance to Port Colborne that would be 14 to 17 feet. [DOT] Did not the weight of the material that was originally excavated at the summit level and piled on each side of the bank, force the bottom up a little ?

There is no doubt it did, and that is part of the work that it is necessary to do. This work has to a considerable degree been increased by the fact that the banks which were constructed under the supervision of the hon. gentlemen opposite in that particular way, have forced up the bottom of the canal.
That would not be true with respect to that portion where there has been rock excavation.
None of it is rock excavation.

It is a fact that a portion of this work is rock excavation. If the hon. gentleman had been here last night he would have learned that fact, and that there was a contract let for that work at $2.90 per cubic yard.
IMr. HAGGART. On the summit level of the Welland canal ?
Yes, at Port Colborne.
On the summit level it must be all clay.
From Port Colborne for about two miles and a half down the canal to what is known as Ramey's Bend, it is all rock excavation. The whole canal Is built through rock, and that has to be deepened.
You have 17 feet on the mitre sill of the lock, what is the depth of the excavation for Port Colborne harbour, that part which is under the control of the Canals Department.
The harbour is 22 feet, we reduced it at the entrance to the lock to 17 feet.
What is the standard you take for 22 feet depth ? Is it the original bench mark of the canal ?
It is the original design.
Are you making allowance in your 22 feet excavation for Port Colborne, for the variation caused by the lowering of Lake Erie which the hon. gentleman mentions ?
Just the same as it is done in the canal.
Just the same as it is being done on this level of the canal ?
Yes.
You are taking the 22 feet navigation of Port Colborne, is that on the new depth or the new bench mark allowing for the lowering of the water in Lake Erie ?

The jurisdiction of the Department of Railways and Canals only extends to the outer extremity of the pier at Port Colborne. From the outer end of the pier, the beginning of the jurisdiction of the Department of Railways and Canals, the depth of the canal will be probably 15 feet on the whole summit level. Outside of that is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works, who, I understand, are making a basin there with a depth of 22 feet under any condition of weather, so that the largest boats on the upper lakes can go into the elevator and unload no matter what the climatic conditions may be as respects the wind.

I understood entirely different. I understood that part of the work of deepening that was in process at Port Colborne, was under the jurisdiction of the Canals Department, that outside the locks they are deepening to the extent of 22 feet in order that vessels may come up to Port Colborne, and over this portion they have jurisdiction ; or do you only take jurisdiction to the end of the lock ?
To the end of the pier.
Does the Department of Public Works have jurisdiction to the guard lock of the canal ?
Not up to the guard lock.

The harbour itself is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works ; the channel which runs from the harbour into the entrance of the canal is under the control of the Department of Railway and Canals.
Are you deepening that channel 22 feet or only 17 ?

I am informed by the chief engineer that they are deepening that channel to 22 feet.
Elevator at Port Colborne, including foundation, $310,000.

The estimated cost of the elevator and foundations, including the machinery for operating and handling grain is $1,110,000. The capacity is 2,000,000 bushels. The foundations and superstructure were designed and planned by J. A. Jamieson, of Montreal, an acknowledged expert in this special line of engineering, and who is paid a commission of five per cent for the same, including superintendence during construction. The elevator will be fire proof, being constructed principally of steel and concrete. Mr. Jamieson has designed elevators for the Canadian Pacific Railway at Owen Sound and St. John, and for the Montreal Transportation Company at Kingston and other places. We have let the contract for the foundations, the contract price at schedule rates amounting to $95,200.
Has the hon. minister considered the possibility of having these elevators made of tile instead of iron? The iron ones are found to be affected more by the heat in summer and the cold in winter.

This is not completely iron, but concrete and iron. It is different from the ordinary iron elevators. It is a new design of elevator in accordance with the most modern ideas and is to be one of the most up to date elevators that is to be found on this continent.
They are all that.
They may be.
A concrete elevator erected at Duluth some years ago is more or less a failure and the iron elevators are failures.
This is a combination of the two.
What is the policy of the government in reference to these elevators? What is the object of building them and what are you going to do with them after they are built?

This is, of course, for the storage of grain. A harbour has been constructed at Port Colborne at great expense. Vast sums of public moneys have been expended there. There were quite a number of applications received by the department from time to time from transportation companies and other private corporations asking for the privilege of putting up separate elevators on the public works at that point at the entrance to the canal. It was deemed in the public interest better for Canada to furnish a large elevator which would be open to the general public m accordance with certain regulations and subject to conditions and tolls. It was deemed that it would be better that Canada should

expend tlie money to construct this elevator and give to all who are interested in the transportation question an opportunity of availing themselves of elevator facilities. Thus it was that it was determined to construct this elevator. It will be the largest elevator, as far as I have any knowledge, in Canada, and will certainly meet the present and even anticipated requirements of the traffic from the west to the east by the lakes.
Last session when the hon. gentleman was taking a vote he asked for about $40,000 for the purpose of constructing the foundations of this elevator.
$400,000 was asked for last year.
But $40,000 for the foundations.
We asked for $400,000 last year. At that time it was anticipated that we would have the foundations further advanced, but in consequence of the delay-

It appears in the estimates that you asked for $400,000 and 1 want to state what the hon. minister said last year in reference to it. He wanted $40,000 for the foundations for this elevator. He stated that in the course of the construction of the piers it would be necessary, whether the elevator was erected by private enterprise or by the government, to build the foundations. Last year the government had not decided whether it would be better for private individuals to build this elevator or whether the government should have control of it. It was a moot question with the government; they did not know whether they would expend a dollar or not in reference to this matter. What is the advantage of having this elevator built by the government and interfering with what ought to be strictly and purely a private enterprise ? What was the reason that induced the government to build this elevator?

Well I would say to my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) that as far as my judgment is concerned it was to prevent one or two transportation companies getting the control of that waterway. There can only of necessity be a limited number of elevators and they would be under the control of the exclusive few. There would be a large majority of those engaged in lake transportation who would be entirely shut out, and, of course, the expenditure of public moneys there is supposed to be in the general interest. It is for the good of the greatest number, and if it were our policy to permit private parties to have the use of the works there for their particular private business it would not promote the general lake traffic. The government believe that the application of this principle must commend itself to those who are interested in getting the traffic from the Mr. EMMERSON.
west to the east and while it cannot be said to be a money making enterprise in view of the expected traffic, it need not be a money losing operation.

Then, you are going into what is after all an individual or private enterprise on the ground that perhaps a couple of parties might erect elevators at Port Colborne and interfere with what might not be in the interest of the general public. That is the reason stated by the hon. minister for this arrangement. He says that in the interest of the general public the control of this elevator should be in the hands of the government because it might tend to monopoly in the hands of private individuals. I suppose the hon. minister has the report which he sent to Council or at least the report of his deputy urging the reasons why the government should build this particular elevator. Within a few miles of Port Colborne there is centered a great amount of traffic requiring the greatest elevator capacity in any part of the world. Yet, I am not aware that either the state of New York or the government of the United States has interfered with what should be purely private enterprise by having an elevator erected in Buffalo or in any part or portion of the United States. It is a new venture for governments to enter the domain of private enterprise for the purpose of erecting elevators in the interest of the public, in the hope that it will accrue to the public advantage afterwards. It is true that on the Intercolonial Railway as part' and portion of that railway we have erected elevators, mostly in places where grain never reaches them, like Halifax, and to a certain extent St. John, and we have, for the convenience of the Intercolonial Railway or perhaps for some reason on the lines the hon. gentleman advances, erected one in Quebec, but if the government of the country are going to furnish elevators for every part of the Dominion of Canada where it might be to the public interest and advantage that elevators should be erected they are opening up a very wide field indeed. What is the cost of this elevator going to be?

My hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) cannot have forgotten the proposition made to this parliament last year, that it would be in the public interest to build elevators along the railways as a public charge and under the control of the public. This proposition is a natural sequence of the action of this parliament in building the breakwater at the entrance to the Welland canal in the harbour of Port Colborne. A very large sum of money was expended in the public interest-wisely expended we must assume-in order to facilitate the lake traffic. In order to have any traffic whatever, it is necessary to have an elevator there. There are conflicting interests, competitive companies, all disputing for the

right to enjoy the major portion of that traffic, or all of it that they can get. There can only be a limited number of elevators, probably two at the most, placed upon these public works. If one or two of these companies secured these elevators, then where would be the facilities that other companies are seeking for ? They would be simply shut out. and the large sums of the money of Canada which have been expended in the erection of that breakwater and the building up of that harbour would have been expended in order that one or two companies should have a monopoly of the traffic. That would be simply placing the expenditure of this large sum of money at their disposal, shutting out the larger number of transportation companies. It seems to me that these are very good reasons for the action proposed to be taken by the government with respect to this large elevator, which will be open to the public at large.

The minister has a curious system of ratiocination, which I am not able to follow. He says that the natural sequence of building a breakwater, if the public are going to utilize it, would be to furnish it with an elevator for the benefit of the public ; in order to derive any benefit from the deepening of Port Colborne harbour and the entrance to the mouth of the Welland canal and to utilize it to the fullest extent in the interest of the public, we have to erect the largest elevator on the continent of America, and we do it probably for the reason that there is only room for two elevators there. It is news to most of us that you can only erect two elevators in that large harbour which is being constructed at Port Colborne, and that if the two were erected the public would be at the mercy of the elevator owners. It is in the interest of the public, it is the natural sequence, according to the hon. gentleman's style of argument, that when you erect a breakwater, and desire to use it to the fullest extent, you have to erect also an elevator for the benefit of the public at large. There should be an end of this kind of thing; something should be left to private enterprise in this country. The natural sequence, according to the minister's argument, of the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific by the government would be that we should erect elevators on the line of the different railways that are in operation throughout the country.

There is no doubt a question involved which is of very great public importance in the construction of the elevator at Port Colborne. There is a contingent on the opposite side of the House in this parliament who believe that the government should own all these utilities, not only the elevators, but all the railways, telegraph lines and telephone lines in the country. Possibly this government is starting, in a small way, in that direction by owning
the elevator at Port Colborne and, perhaps, in other places. Whether it is wise for the government to own the elevator, or whether that should be left to private enterprise, is a matter for discussion ; for myself, I am free to admit that I desired the government to allow a private company to construct this elevator. But the rights claimed by private companies were rather ' extreme. In the first place, Mr. Wolvin, of Duluth, who is the head of a large transportation company which operates between Duluth and the head of Lake Superior and Montreal and Quebec, desired to have the right to construct an elevator or elevators at Port Colborne. The government, some years ago, began, and have nearly completed, the construction of two large concrete piers at Port Colborne, which are being constructed exclusively for the purpose of erecting on them elevators and storage warehouses at considerable expense. It was thought to be in the public interest that this should be done, and I do not know that there has been any serious criticism of the government's action in the construction of these works. In order to make these works of any benefit to the country, elevators had to be built. Mr. Wolvin desired the right to construct an elevator on one of these piers, but he insisted that if he did anything he should have an exclusive right. Certain financial gentlemen in Toronto applied to parliament for a charter, and I had the honour of fathering their Bill. Hon. gentlemen can see from the Bill who the incorporators are, some of the wealthiest men in Toronto. Their idea was to get the rigflit from this government, if possible, to construct an elevator or elevators at Port Colborne, and to put on a line of boats of canal size to carry grain on the lake route to Montreal. But these gentlemen, before they would go into the enterprise, before they would even think of constructing an elevator, insisted upon having a monopoly or an exclusive right to build elevators. They said that the matter was experimental, and that it was in the nature of a gamble, to expend large sums of money in the construction of ships and in the building of elevators at Port Colborne, terminals at Montreal and Quebec. They said that if they spent this large sum of money, they must have the exclusive right to the use of the elevators at Port Colborne. Mr. Wolvin insisted on the same thing. These two companies came into competition ; they came to the government; Mr. Wolvin insisted on the exclusive right to construct the elevators, and the company of Canadian capitalists which was incorporated here also insisted on an exlusive right. The government decided-wisely or otherwise, is a question for argument-that rather than give any company the exclusive right to construct and control these elevators, the government would build an elevator itself. The government is going on to build the elevator, and I have no fear but that the

future will demonstrate conclusively that the construction of this elevator will aid very materially in the solution of the transportation question in Canada, and bring about the transportation of grain through Canadian channels instead of through American channels, where it goes at present.
Does the minister know the amount of grain which has gone through the Welland canal during the present year as compared with previous years ? Has there been any increase ?

We have an interim report, it seems now, from the commissioners who were appointed to investigate our transportation facilities? I understood from the answer that was given in the House the other day that there were no reports.

It has been stated here more than once that this commission, under the chairmanship of the late Mr. Bertram, had reported with respect to the St. ,Tohn harbour, and, if I mistake not, that report was laid before parliament. It was also stated, if I mistake not, at the last session, that the matter of the Port Colborne harbour facilities was being inquired into by this commission, and that they proposed making an interim report, and they did so.
Are these all the reports you have from the commission ? .

Speaking from memory, there are only two. The commission went to St. John, Halifax and Sydney, if I mistake not. At any rate" they went to St. John and they have made a report with respect to that harbour and a report with respect to Port Colborne. I do not think they have made any other suggestions-certainly not a general report.

It would be most interesting to the committee to have a report from that transportation commission. I had every faith in the ability of the chairman of that commission, who has died, and a report from him would be of great use to this committee. When we are considering the expenditure of two or three million dollars for the building of elevators at Port Colborne and the deepening of the harbour and that portion of the canal which reaches the harbour, we ought to have the full report of the commission on the subject. We ought to be informed how the traffic is going to be diverted, what rates are going to be charged on these elevators, and how, the whole affair is going to result commercially. We know nothing about any of these matters. The minister should furnish us with a tabulated statement showing mathematically the commercial advantages si what the government propose to do.

The hon. gentleman asks for an accurate statement showing the commercial advantages. Let me invite his attention to the situation, and it he will take a comprehensive view of it he will see that it is our duty to erect this elevator regardless whether it will pay in the matter of fees, because its erection is essential to the utilization of the enormous capital we have already expended on the Welland canal. That canal has a carrying capacity of 14 feet. I believe that the locks are able to lock through vessels carrying about 70.000 bushels. But every one knows that on the upper lakes to-day are plying a

large number of grain carrying vessels of a capacity of 200,000 bushels and more, some going as high as 300,000.
Drawing what water ?
Twenty feet.
Nineteen feet.

Those vessels are to-day doing the chief carrying trade on the lakes, carrying grain from Duluth and Fort William down chiefly to Buffalo. Why do they not bring it to Port Colborne ? Those vessels carry sufficient cargo to fill at least four or five canal barges the full capacity of the lakes, and they will not come to Port Colborne if they have to be detained there. They must feel sure, when they start from Duluth or Fort William, that they will be able at once, on reaching Port Colborne, to unload either into barges or elevators. We have built a breakwater and dredged and deepened the harbour inside the breakwater. There are five hundred acres, or nearly a mile square of harbour safe for these vessels, but to-day they must give it the go-by and go to Buffalo because there are no facilities at Port Colborne to enable them to discharge their cargoes at once and immediately return. It is the very essence of the carrying trade that these vessels should utilize every moment of time during the short season of navigation instead of having to wait idly for hours or days before starting on their return trip. There are between 200 and 300 of these vessels on the upper lakes bringing the grain from the upper ports to Buffalo, and these vessels give the go-by to Port Colborne simply because we have not the facilities for unloading at the port which they require. The erection of an elevator there is therefore absolutely essential if we want to bring the traffic to that port and down the Welland canal. We have spent $60,000,000 from first to last on our canals, and they have not yet at all realized the expectations of our people or given any direct or indirect reasonable return on that expenditure. Why is this ? Simply because the key to the situation is Port Colborne, and that port has not yet been equipped in such a way as to make it possible for us to capture that traffic. If we are to enjoy the fruition of the expenditure on our canals, which has been justified by public opinion ever since confederation, we must completely equip that port. My hon. friend possibly takes exception to the government, but what is the situation ? If Port Colborne is the key to the situation, we must not imperil our chances by giving the control of the elevator at that port to any one person or company. There is not unlimited space there ; and if we were to give any set of gentlemen the building of the elevator, they would acquire a quasi monopoly and possibly deter others from investing money there in like manner.
We know what wheels there are within wheels and how combines and organizations grow up. If we were to allow a set of men to build an elevator at Port Colbornei it might pay them better to shut up the elevator. They might make more money by playing into the hands of Buffalo ; and while you make agreements-my experience of agreements with great corporations

Be careful.
Sir WILLIAM MULOCK-is that in some way or other these corporations are able largely to evade the most carefully drawn bargains.
Would the hon. minister mind letting us into the secret of how they do this ?

I am sure I could not add anything to the hon. gentle^ man's information on that question. In my opinion the only way for us to be safe is for the government to own this elevator. Then the grain men of Buffalo could not, as theyi might in case the elevator were owned by a private company, use their influence to have this elevator closed or its usefulness defeated. If a company should own the elevator, they might probably conform to the letter of the agreement and yet defeat its spirit. They might have a slow method of handling the grain. They might embarrass the boats coming and going. They might in many ways injure the trade without actually violating the agreement. On the other hand if the government should be the owner, they will have no interest except to bring the largest volume of trade through the elevator so as to make our canals useful and have the country reap the greatest advantage from the money expended. I do not think there can be any argument in favour of private ownership of an elevator at the mouth of Port Colborne as against the arguments in favour of government ownership. We should view with the greatest alarm the giving over the right to own the elevator to any corporation or set of men. The present scheme has my heartiest approval. I believe it will prove the turning point in the history of the Welland canal. That canal has not up to the present realized in any respect the expectations of the people and I shall be disappointed beyond expression if the building of this elevator will not bring to this canal as much grain as it can carry. Without this elevator how could a vessel drawing 19 feet of water come into Port Colborne and be discharged, if the weather be not favourable? If the vessel owners could be sure that when they got to Port Colborne there would be fine weather, they might come in, and a few do occasionally come in, but very few because they cannot depend upon it. True, the breakwater has to some extent got over that difficulty, but then the question of delay

comes in. I am told that when this elevator is constructed, it will give facilities for transhipment at Port Colborne that will enable vessels carrying 150,000 bushels of. grain to unload and leave the harbour in six hours less than they could in Buffalo harbour. I do not know what the difficulties are in that harbour.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The time taken in getting there and back.
It is not only that, but there are difficulties there.
Congestion in the harbour.

There are other difficulties 1 understand. My authority is an engineer, I think it was Mr. Weller. I visited Port Colborne harbour and talked with the men in the government service there, and they gave me to understand that a vessel of the kind I speak of would be able to save six hours on each trip. That is a very material saving, I suppose, in a short season of navigation. So, if we have the elevator there, we have the chance of having between two and three hundred vessels drawing 19 feet of water or thereabouts coming to our harbour with traffic, while, to-day, we have not a chance of any of them coming. Surely, the prospect is a favourable one. How else are you going to get the trade ? If you do not put up an elevator, you get along in the same miserable way as in the past. We have had enough disappointment in the working of the canal and it is time to display such enterprise as will actually bring the traffic our way. Everything is done except the finishing of the work. We have spent $60,000,000, and surely we are not going to stop at an expense of $2,000,000 if by that expenditure we have a fair chance of securing the trade.

I asked the minister (Sir William Mulock) if he would give us light on the matter of large companies controlling the elevators. I do not know that he has thrown light on anything, but, if he has, it is certainly not on the subject before the House. He speaks of two or three hundred vessels drawing 19 feet of water coming from Port Arthur and Port William to Port Colborne. He says he does not know anything about the grain-shipping business. I can tell him that if he is going to get two or three hundred vessels from Port Arthur and Port William, they must be American vessels, and they could not carry freight from Port William to Port Colborne.
Why not ?

Because they are American ships and are not allowed to engage in coasting traffic. That is, they are not allowed to go from one Canadian port direct to another. They could not be Canadian boats, because there are not nearly Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
that number of Canadian boats drawing 19 feet of water.
We will get the Duluth traffic.
The hon. minister spoke of Port Arthur and Fort William and did not mention Duluth.
Yes, I did.

I did not hear him. In the shipping of this grain it is not a race to reach Port Colborne or Buffalo. The question is how to send the grain most quickly and most cheaply from Duluth, Port Arthur or Port William to its final destination. Buffalo is nearly the end of the shipping route, where the grain is taken hold of by the various railways-very little of it goes by the Erie canal and little will go by the Welland canal. The minister says we have no place to receive the grain. Why, Midland is a great deal nearer Duluth, Port Arthur and Port William than Port Colborne is.
I did not make that statement.
I do not think the minister knew what statement he was making. He said we had no place to receive the grain
No, I made no such statement.

At any rate we have Midland which is a deeper harbour and much nearer Chicago and Duluth and Port Arthur than Port Colborne is. There are elevators there and a railway connection that will take the grain to the sea-board at cheaper rates than can be given from Port Colborne. In a short time we shall have the item for the Trent canal under consideration. I hope the government will push that work through to completion. We shall then have the grain carried to the sea-board by a sheltered route all the way. I trust that in a few years we shall have the Georgian bay canal via Lake Nipissing and the French river. This will be another sheltered route for grain to the sea-board and will make it unnecessary to go round the circuitous route by way of Port Colborne. I am not finding fault with the expenditure under consideration. I believe the scheme to be all moonshine, but I have never opposed it. If there is anything in the theory that this can be made a great shipping route I am willing to try it. But, I must say, I cannot see how any shipper of grain is going to ship to Port Colborne, then place the grain in small vessels to send it by canal, or send it in cars, to Lake Ontario, then load it into boats and take it to Montreal. The barge trade on Lake Ontario cannot be made a success. I believe it would be better to enlarge the Welland canal and let the vessels go through

to Montreal, rather than waste money in building up Port Colborne.

One fact the effect of which was not fully realized, I believe in before the enormous expenditure at Port Colborne was decided upon is that the grain shipped by the Welland canal is destined to be exported by the St. Lawrence route. This route closes comparatively early and at the very time when grain is being shipped to Buffalo in the largest quantities. The last boat from Montreal carrying grain leaves about November 10th. That is, the shipper from Port Arthur, Fort William or Duluth cannot rely upon sending out his grain by Montreal unless he gets it through the Welland canal and into the port of Montreal not later than that date. The greatest rush of grain is between the beginning of November and the middle of December, and the closing of navigation from Port Arthur is certainly uot earlier than December Gth. This year vessels left Port Arthur loaded with grain and landed their cargoes at Georgian bay ports-I think I am right in saying-up to December 10th.
The Welland canal closes on December 15th usually.

I am not speaking of the Welland canal, but of the destination of the grain that goes by the Welland canal-that grain is destined for export by the St. Lawrence, and, as I say, it must reach Montreal not later than November 10th. I am a little familiar with vessel trade on the lakes and am aware that the boats are being made of greater and greater capacity every year. The boat that was considered a large boat four years ago Is one that would not now be built by any one going into the grain trade. The whole object that the grain men have in view, so far as I can ascertain, is to build as large boats as possible and land their grain on the eastern shore of the Georgian bay. If the enormous expenditure at Port Colborne realizes in any degree the hopes built upon it, I shall be delighted. I am quite willing that whatever amount is necessary to the carrying out of any reasonable project should be spent. But I am afraid that tiie conditions of our canal navigation will render the usefulness of this expenditure doubtful to say the least of it. All the railways, the Grand Trunk Pacific, Mackenzie & Mann and the Canadian Pacific Railway are looking to get increased facilities on the eastern side of the Georgian bay, so that they may as rapidly as possible get rid of their wheat from Port Arthur and Fort William. The railways do not wish to have a bushel of grain lying in the elevators on the west side of Lake Superior when navigation closes, and they want boats that will empty the elevators and transfer the grain to the eastern side of the lakes that it may be carried away even in the winter. I believe that the ministers in going into this
enormous expenditure at Port Colborne have not realized the fact that the grain goes to Buffalo not so much because of superior advantages of that harbour itself-though they have superior advantages we admit-but because the grain can be distributed from Buffalo six weeks later than it can be from Port Colborne. I think that is the secret of the Buffalo grain trade. Furthermore we find that about two-thirds of the grain shipped to Buffalo is distributed through the state of New York and the New England states and is not exported. Say that 300, 000,000 bushels of grain are received at Buffalo, that is quoted as grain that should have gone down from the Welland canal and through our ports. But if you trace that grain out you will find that less than 100,000,000 bushels perhaps not more than one-fourth of the whole, is for export ; the balance of it is used up in New York city and in the New England states. I think when we are discussing the question of the Welland canal as against Buffalo, we are apt to omit that important consideration. I do not think we sufficiently realize that the main reason why Port Colborne and the Welland canal do not take the traffic that we think they ought to take, is because the grain traffic comes too late to he carried by that route.
Sir WILLIAM MULOCIC It is to be borne in mind that the government is not to-day originating the scheme of the Welland canal. That was determined upon a third of a century ago, or more. We find ourselves to-day confronted with a situation. The Welland canal is completed to 11 feet, that was a policy adopted by the previous government, and we have simply adhered to it, and brought the depth of the St. Lawrence locks to that depth of 14 feet. Now, because it is possible that other routes are more suitable, are we to stop and allow the Welland canal to fall into decay ? Are we to say it is a failure, instead of giving it the finishing touch so that it may have a chance ? That is the situation. If we had not the Welland canal to-day, and if we had the existing railways, and route, and ideas, perhaps the country would pause before embarking in a Wei-land canal at all. But the canal has been built. Is it-wise therefore for us to decide that it is a failure and not give it a chance? It may be that climate, it may be that geography is against us, but I am not quite prepared to admit that. As time goes on we may expect that transportation rates will become cheaper, and then grain can go through the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence canals and will be able to reach the eastern market before the close of navigation. Perhaps the Minister of Railways will be able to take it by his railway to a maritime port. We have not yet learned at what cheap rates grain can be hauled by railway. But even if we had to lose a few days, even if our outport should become congested, or the vessels should leave too

soon, is that any reason why we should not try to bring the grain down as far as we can ? What reason is there to suppose that during the early period of navigation, with the several hundred vessels that are now bringing grain to Buffalo, you cannot bring cargoes by the Canadian route if they can unload within the proper time ? My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) says that if at that late date in the season they can with greater advantage bring their grain to Buffalo, they will do it. But that does not prevent them at an earlier date in the season unloading at Port Colborne. At all events, if you do not have a harbour at Port Colborne you cannot have the trade. Is there any person in this House who would say that we should not have a harbour at Port Colborne and give that port a chance ? Even if nobody contested that view, then it is only a question of detail as to what we should do in order to give the Welland canal a chance. We must have a breakwater, everybody concedes that. You have to deepen the harbour for vessels drawing 30 feet of water, and you have to have some machinery for handling the grain. It is not a question of choice. There is the necessity, you are confronted with a situation from which you cannot escape. You have either to provide facilities at Port Colborne, or you might as well close up the Welland canal. That is my view of the situation.

I do not object to the expenditure of money, in fact I approve of it to an almost unlimited extent if it will heighten the facilities for carrying our grain to market. But I do not approve of the Postmaster General's premises, that because we have spent an enormous amount of money on a route that may be superseded, we must continue to expend it.
I did not make a general remark, I was addressing myself to a particular work.

If it can be found that by spending $500,000 or $600,000 on some other harbour which will accomplish our object, it wpuld be much better expended than it is there, notwithstanding that a large amount of money has been spent on the Welland canal. The tendency is to get as short a run as possible from the Lake Superior side to the Georgian bay or eastern side. That is the object all vessels have, that is the reason they are building bigger vessels ; and an enormous increase in the business will take place when the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Mackenzie & Mann roads are in operation. I do not think the government sufficiently weigh this matter, or give sufficient attention to this question, if they are only spending more money on the Welland canal because, as the Postmaster General says, we have already spent so much. I do not think that is a good argument at all.

I am a firm believer in waterways, that is the proper way of carrying our grain to the sea. In considering this proposed vote of a sum of money to deepen the Welland canal, the real question is not whether it is right and proper to put an elevator there, but is this a proper amount to pay for that elevator. As I understand it, $95,000 is asked for to build the foundations for an elevator that can only carry 1,000,000 bushels of grain.

Well, say 2,000,000. Now at Owen Sound it costs 13 cents a bushel to build an elevator, in the city of Buffalo, where the foundations are in mud, it costs 20 cents. The question is whether we should build an elevator there or not. There is no question that we should spend money on our waterways. The United States are considering the question of expending $100,000,000 on the Erie canal. We have a much shorter canal to carry grain. We should spend the money on our harbours. We should spend money on the Welland canal, so as to enable it to take care of the grain traffic. In 1902, 12,000,000 bushels of grain went through Buffalo because of the want of facilities to carry it through our own country. This government should promote the public interests by building up our waterways. We are spending too much money elsewhere. We should spend it on our great lakes and inland waterways. We have the best of facilities, if our waterways were improved, for handling the traffic through the Welland canal and by way of Montreal, and I want to say to the committee that last year and the year before, grain was carried from Duluth to Quebec at one and a half cents a bushel by the Wolvin steamers through the Welland canal. I would be glad if the government could see their way clear to deepening the Welland canal. I wish to ask the hon. minister whether this is a proper amount to be expended on the erection of an elevator and whether this work is to be let by tender. Private corporations, when doing similar work, adopt the principle of tender and contract. The Canadian Pacific Railway have built elevators at Owen Sound and at Fort William. I believe that they paid for a first-class elevator 13 cents a bushel at the outside. Canada should have a twenty-foot waterway from Fort William to Montreal.

If all the advantages from the expenditure at Port Colborne entailed by the erection of this elevator that my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) anticipates, were likely to be realized I am sure that the House and the country would have no objection to this vote. Let us see what the position is. In order to utilize the waterways we have at present he says that further facilities should be offered. We have constructed a harbour at Port Colborne a mile square with a

depth of 22 feet of water and there are only facilities for the erection of two elevators within that mile square. We all know about the harbour at Port Colborne, and we are aware that the difficulty of getting into the harbour was one of the objections to it. That is the reason perhaps why a good deal of the traffic was diverted to Buffalo. If you want to utilize the Welland canal without the deepening of Port Colborne harbour or the erection of an elevator why do you not send your barges to Buffalo and load them with the grain from the steamers there? Any steamer navigating the western lakes would rather go to Buffalo than to Port Colborne.
Why?
The facilities for getting to Buffalo are much better than, notwithstanding your breakwater, Port Colborne will ever offer.
Why are the facilities for getting to Buffalo better ?
I will tell you why. When there is a wind blowing on Lake Erie, Port Colborne is a difficult and dangerous harbour to enter.
There was no harbour at that place.

The facilities you are providing do not remove the objections at all. They do to a certain extent but not altogether. However, If you want to utilize the Welland canal to the fullest extent why not load your barges at Buffalo where the steamers at present terminate their journey? What is the objection to it? You have a few miles more of a journey at a cost which Is infinitesimal. Now, the main question to be considered is this: a party has grain at Chicago, Duluth or Fort William which he wants to send to the sea-board. He goes to the stock exchange and asks: What can I get that grain to Liverpool for ? He does not care two cents whether it goes by way of New York, Baltimore, New Orleans, Montreal, or any other point. I quoted statistics here a couple of years ago to show that a fraction of a cent per bushel changes the destination of millions of bushels of grain from one port to another. Then, I ask the very pertinent question : Of what commercial advantage is the erection of an elevator at Port Colborne and the deepening of the harbour to the man sending grain from Duluth, Fort William or Chicago ? I thought perhaps that question would be the first that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals would ask of his department so as to be able to tell the committee the advantages which would accrue to the people of this country from the deepening of the harbour at Port Colborne and the erection of an elevator there: It seems to me he has not considered that question. I think this is the first and most 41-
pertinent question that can be asked in connection with the expenditure which we are asked to make of nearly $3,000,000. The expenditure involved in the deepening of Port Colborne harbour is not for the advantage of the Welland canal at all. The depth of water in the Welland canal for navigation purposes is 14 feet. They have a depth of 20 feet 6 inches at the Soo canal and the standard of navigation for that section of the country in American waters is 20 feet. What do you expend $3 000,000 or nearly $4,000,000 at Port Colborne for ?- to allow these vessels coming from the upper lakes to get into Port Colborne and tranship. Why could not these facilities already be given fifteen miles further down. This is a large expenditure for that purpose, an enormous expenditure and I doubt very much whether the facilities which are being provided by it will ever be utilized. The government ought to utilize what we have already paid an enormous sum of money for ; that is for the purpose of enlarging our canals. As my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) said, you must remember one thing when you consider the question of diverting traffic. You must know how much traffic there is to be diverted. Look at the exports of grain from Baltimore, New York, New Orleans and other American ports and find out how much really goes from these ports.- You would be astonished to find that the total exports of wheat or the product of wheat from the United States to foreign ports do not amount to 100,000,000 bushels. Then, what do you intend to do? They are building canals for what ? For the foreign market ? They are building canals for the purpose of utilizing their own grain in their own country. As my hon. friend from Toronto says, four-fifths, yes, nineteen-twentieths of the products that pass through the Sault Ste. Marie canal and Lake Superior are consumed in the United States. What is consumed in that country cannot be diverted by any means whatever. You have to consider what would be used in this country and what portion of the traffic goes to foreign countries, or countries across the ocean that you can divert by offering facilities through your own country. You can divert the whole of the traffic from Chicago, Milwaukee and other western points if you go on to the stock exchange and quote to parties in London, Antwerp, Paris or Hamburg grain or any of the products of grain at half a cent per hundred pounds less because they do not care one cent what country it goes through.
-Sir WILLIAM MULOCK. They will get a better rate ?

If they get a better rate through this country, you will divert the trade. You have to offer facilities1 through this country, and the government, when asking for a vote for such a large,



sum as this, should be prepared with a commercial proposition to show the advantages of these expenditures and what would be their effect. That is what I asked the Minister of Railways.
Does the hon. gentleman think that providing proper facilities at Port Colborne would or would not enable shippers to offer a better rate so far as that port is concerned '!

Yes, you incur an expenditure of $4,000,000 and it may be possible to divert a portion of traffic by the expenditure of a million dollars for elevators. The reasoning and logic of the Minister of Railways was that if you make an expenditure for any facilities of that kind-you erect a breakwater and as a necessary sequence have to go on with all the other utilities, and have to erect an elevator for im stance in the harbour. I do not think that the expenditure at Port Colborne for the deepening of the harbour or the erection of an elevator will be at all compensated for by the benefit derived from it. I think you are going the wrong way in reference to your 'tuansportation (expenditure.
What would the hon. gentleman's plan be ?

If the hon. minister bad listened to me I bad a scheme which I explained to the fullest possible extent and I showed the advantages of it. I am not against the minister to a certain extent in his reasoning. We have these facilities at present, we might have used them and by a moderate expenditure we could probably have made them more useful, but I say that the expenditure which has been made now is an abnormal one.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

House went into Committee on Bill (No. 12) respecting the Ottawa Electric Company. -Mr. Galliher.
On section 1,
Mr. LOUIS LAVERGNE moved that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

I was going to rise, before that motion was made, to point out that no one is here to-night representing the city of Ottawa. I am surprised that the members for Ottawa are not present. Perhaps they understood that the Bill was not to come up to-night. I wish to say Mr. HAGGART.
that a number of us have been here night after night to discuss this Bill, and it has been put over from time to time. In justice to a large portion of the community who are interested in this Bill outside of the city of Ottawa, a day ought to be set for the discussion of the Bill. We ought not to be obliged to come here night after night expecting to state our views with regard to this Bill, only to find it put off. If this happens again, some of us will have to bring up the matter in the House, and have some new rule made in regard to these Bills ; because It is very unfair that a Bill of this kind, which some of us consider prejudicial to the public interest, is skipped night after night without any reason being given, and then when there is an available opportunity, or those who are opposed to the Bill are absent, an effort is made to railroad it through. The government must take the responsibility of the repeated postponements of this Bill. While I am quite willing that the committee should rise and report pro-i gress, I think some notice should be given by the promoters of the Bill of the day on which they intend to bring it up.

As this Bill was called to stand by the hon. Postmaster General on the last occasion when the order was called, it wTas thought by some that the government had decided on some course of action regarding it; and therefore it was the more surprising to-night to find so few members present, and especially to find both of the members for Ottawa absent, who above all others are interested in the Bill. I think the committee should rise and report progress, because the Bill is too important to be proceeded with when there is such a slim House as there is to-night.

It was simply as a matter of courtesy I asked that the Bill should stand, when I looked around and saw that the promoter was not here. It was in that spirit that I did so, nothing more or less. I would not desire an act of courtesy on my part to any member of the House to be misconstrued, as it appears to be by the hon. member for East Grey. I was speaking for nobody, but simply did an act of courtesy to an absent member.

I think the minister who is leading the House to-night realizes that Bills of this kind, which concern the vital interests of the people, ought not to come up unless public notice is given. If they are the first on the order paper for a certain day, that is sufficient, if they are proceeded with on that day ; but when they are continually postponed until there is a favourable House and they can be railroaded through, there ought to be a rule that such Bill cannot be called unless some previous notice has been given.
Motion agreed to, and committee rose and reported progress.

House went into Committee on Bill (No. 27) respecting certain patents of the Facer Solid Steel Car Company, of Perth, Limited. -Mr. Caldwell.
On section 1,
Has the government, as representing the Department of Patents, passed upon this Bill, or is the government willing that it should go through ?

I wish to suggest that as there are two or three other Bills of a somewhat similar character to this one, action on all these Bills should be deferred for the present. I know that certain parties desire to be heard in regard to other Bills of a similar nature before they are disposed of. I therefore desire to ask the promoter of this Bill not to press it until we have opportunity to look into it further.

The Minister of Agriculture ought to be here when a Bill of this kind is being considered. I deprecate the continual absence of ministers. The ministers who are responsible for the matters dealt with in these private Bills ought to be present and prepared to enlighten the committee upon them. I think this Bill should stand over until the Minister of Agriculture is in his place.

Since it has been suggested by my hon. friend that consideration of the Bill should be deferred, I think the committee might accede to that view. It is quite right that ministers should as much as possible be in their seats. It is also right that private members should be in their seats. I am afraid that on many occasions the seat of the hon. member for South York is vacant.
Not when anything in which I am interested is up.

Frequently. It was only the other day that he cafne over to this side of the House and begged us to put off something so that he might be present when it came up. We agreed to put it off, because we always deplore his absence.

Allow me to explain what the hon. Postmaster General has referred to. I was in my place by arrangement with the Minister of Justice, but by reason of some action of a colleague of his, the matter that he had arranged to come up had to go over. The minister then said he was willing to make an arrangement with me and fix a day, so that everybody would know when the matter would come up ; and it was because he was not there that I went to one of his colleagues and stated my case. I am always here when Bills in which I am interested come up.
41i
But the hon. member should be here every time.

Much more so should the Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister and all the members of his government. This is on a line with what I brought up this afternoon. There is far too much absence of ministers.
And members.
MACLEAN, Can the hon. gentleman tell us where the Minister of the Interior is to-night ? Who has seen him since this session opened ?
The hon. gentleman knows that he is absent through illness.
That has not been imparted yet. I thought he went on a hunting expedition.
The First Minister announced his illness yesterday ; but the hon. member for South York was not present.
I was here yesterday. The statement was not so much that he was ill, but that the First Minister did not know when he would be in the House.
He announced his illness, and the hon. gentleman knows of his illness.
In view of what has been stated and in view of the importance of this measure, I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Motion agreed to, and committee rose and reported progress.
House went into committee on Bill (No. 29) respecting the Canada Southern Bridge Company.-Mr. German.
Is the bridge commenced ?

No ; it cannot be commenced until certain leave has been secured from the United States government. The matter was fully considered in the Railway Committee, and the Bill was unanimously concurred in.
We usually provide a time limit for commencing as well as for finishing a work. But in this case the limit is for finishing only.
For the reason that it was dependent upon the consent of the United States government. It was thought advisable simply to provide that it should be finished within seven years.
It gives them five years to get authority from the United States to commence.

The Bill, as it has been furnished to me, gives this corporation a right to commence any time within seven years after the passing of an Act of Congress approving the construction, and they have five years from the passing of this Act in which to obtain that approval-making twelve years allowed for the commencement of the bridge.

Have the government a policy in regard to bridging the Niagara river and the Detroit river ? Is it their policy to facilitate the bridging of these rivers ? Apparently it is, and apparently the Minister of Railways has considered the subject. We see these Bills in regard to bridging these international rivers go through without a declaration of policy on our side ; but, apparently, the American government is very reserved about giving permission to bridge these rivers, so far as their side of it is concerned. While I am in favour of improving traffic facilities and of building bridges, because they are needed for the traffic, there ought to be some policy on the part of our government in regard to the matter, and that policy ought to be announced.

Surely the policy of the government is plain from the position of this Bill. We give our permission to have the bridge built. The company have not been able to get the consent of the United States government. That government, I understand, owing to pressure brought to bear upon them by the shipping interests, have refused permission thus far.
We also have a large shipping interest.
There has been no protest from the shipping interest.

The minister says, then, that the government have considered the matter, and they take the responsibility. That is what I wanted to know.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
