Welland canal-elevator at Port Colborne, including foundations, $310,000.
['Monday, February 20, 1905.']

speakeroldname: Hon. H. R. EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: A good deal has been said by way of making a comparison between the advantages afforded by Port Colborne and the advantages of some other ports, particularly those in the United States. Now while there may be ports which have advantages over our Canadian ports, and while there may be conditions and circumstances more favourable than those which exist in Canada, I do not think that it is in accord with the sentiment of Canadians to-day that we should remain inactive and take no action in the way of availing ourselves of every possible facility for securing at least a portion of the lake traffic. Now the action of the government in connection with the Port Colborne harbour and works has been largely guided by the report of the transportation commission. I had supposed that the report had been laid upon the table, or that its contents were within the knowledge of this committee. That not being the case, it would be fair that the committee should have a knowledge of it, and I shall avail myself of this opportunity to place before the committee the contents of that interim report.
Although that report has been called for twice, we were told it was not available, up to the present.
I had the report in my hand and was waiting an opportunity.
It was called for days ago.
I did not understand the hon. member to make reference to that commission.
It was the leader of the opposition.

We cannot always hear what is said across the floor of the House, and I did not hear any reference made to this report, though no doubt, as the hon. gentleman says, it was called for. Had I heard it called for I could readily have told the hon. member that there were two interim reports, one of which has already been placed before the House of Commons, that relating to the harbour of St. John. The other report is dated at Toronto, May 6, 1904, and is addressed to His Excellency the Governor General
May it' please your Excellency :-
We have the honour to report that in carrying out the work entrusted to us as your com-

missioners on transportation, we visited on the 3rd instant, the town of Port Colborne, Ont., at the inlet of the Welland canal on Lake Brie.
This port, situated at the eastern end of deep water navigation on the upper lakes and at the beginning of the St'. Lawrence system of canals, [DOT]occupies an important position on the water Toute from Port William to Montreal. Passing along a level stretch of the canal from Thorold to Port Colborne, about thirteen miles in length, we were informed by the engineer in charge that between Port Dalhousie and Port Colborne the whole length of the canal had now the full depth of fourteen feet, and that *only two more centre piers required to be taken out' from the bridges over the canal, when there would be no obstruction to any width of vessel passing through.
Arriving at Port Colborne our attention was given to the condition of the harbour and its facilities for furthering transportation by the St. Lawrence channel.
In our examination we were favoured with the assistance and advice of Mr. J. L. Weller, superintending engineer of the Welland canai. Mr. A. J. Grant, the resident engineer at Port Colborne, and Mr. L. Coste, engineer of the Public Works Department.
Around the lake front at Port Colborne the water is shallow and the entrance to the canal has required a great deal of dredging through limestone rock.
The entrance to the canal from the new elevator piers to the guard lock is about 4,600 feet long, with a depth of 16 feet and 230 feet wide, except at the old east pier. Along the north end of this stretch, on both sides, is situated the town of Port Colborne, and on the east side, the small Grand Trunk elevator. At a distance of 4,600 feet from the guard lock, the new elevator piers have been built, the entrance is much wider and opening towards the lake, and all around the piers there is a depth of 22 feet, the rock dredging is still being continued to give ample facilities for steamers turning.
The elevator piers are built of concrete on a Tock foundation, their length being 700 feet by 200 feet wide, with a connecting pier on the north side 200 feet by 100 feet connected by an old pier which needs to be repaired. To the southwest of these new piers a breakwater has been built 4,500 feet long and situated 1,650'feet out into the lake, which will, no doubt, guard the site from any southwest or south storm, but leaving it still exposed to the south-east.
To guard this the Department of Public Works have plans out for another breakwater to the southeast 2,400 feet long, and commencing 600 feet from the eastern end of the present breakwater, which when built will fully shelter the harbour. The question of how to utilize the existing canal system is important enough to merit the most careful consideration.
At the present time, with no facility for discharging cargoes at this port, the use of the route from Fort William to Montreal is confined to steamers drawing not more than fourteen feet and of a size to pass through the locks, giving a maximum capacity of 75,000 bushels of wheat, and to tow barges hauled by tugs or by'steam barges of full canal size, 256 feet long by 42 feet wide, leaving entirely out *of account the large steamers passing through the Sault Ste. Marie canal and carrying 200,000 bushels of U'heat and upwards, able to carry grain on a 20 foot draught of water cheaper than any smaller 'steamer. The building of these larger steamers is a development since the Sault Ste. Marie canal was deepened ; they
have cheapened freights, and if the St. Lawrence route is to have equal opportunities with the American, facilities must be provided for the discharge of cargoes from large steamers at Port' Colborne, from whence it can be sent to Montreal in other Vessels of canal size.
Your commissioners have, therefore, the honour to recommend :-
That the work of putting in a suitable foundation and the erection of an elevator at Port Colborne harbour be proceeded with at once, the capacity to be not less than one million bushels, and placed so that additional storage bins can be added when found necessary. The elevator to be of the most modern and approved type, giving the quickest despatch to vessels loading and unloading, provision also being made for loading railway cars when connection is made. The government to retain the ownership, thus avoiding any possible complication or deflection of traffic from the St. Lawrence route ; the rates for elevation to be as low as possible, the main object being to encourage the route rather than to make a profit for the elevator.
That the old pier stretching from the elevator lighthouse to the shore line, now in a dilapidated condition, should be rebuilt and carried to a depth of 22 feet to provide for future dredging contingencies and that the pier on the east side of the channel spoken of as the old east pier be taken out as an obstruction to navigation.
That action should be taken to have the two remaining centre piers under the railway bridges over the canal removed as soon as possible.
Although there are two piers provided on which to erect elevators, your commissioners will not think it advisable to build more than one at present, have it tested, and see what effect it has in increasing the traffic on the St. Lawrence system, which we feel assured will be so beneficial as to require additional elevator capacity at an early date.
All of which is respectfully submitted, for the commissioners,
(Sgd.) JOHN BERTRAM,
Chairman.
Now, that embodies in very few words and very pointedly the policy of the government in respect to the proposed elevator at Port Colborne, and it seems to me that no more meritorious work could be undertaken by the government in connection with this; canal system. It is not a question as to the existence of the Welland canal. The policy in regard to the Welland canal wag adopted years ago. We must deal with; conditions and circumstances and while exception has been taken to the remarks which I made as to this being a natural sequence, of the expenditure already made I think that if you deal with it from the stand; point of the circumstances and conditions that prevail there no exception can be taken to the conclusions I have arrived at. The expenditure in connection with the entrance to the canals seems to have been preliminary to some such action. There may be a question as to the policy adopted ; that is as to whether the government should build and control this elevator or whether it should be left to private enterprise. It seems to me

that haying regard to the safeguarding of Canadian transportation interests the only proper policy to be pursued is the one adopted by the government in connection with this elevator and X submit that this sum. should be voted by this committee at this time with the view of carrying out that policy.

We have some information from the reading of the report of the commissioners on transportation. If I understood the report as read by the hon, gentleman the distance between the entrance lock and Port Colborne proper, is 4,6O0( feet. Is that so ?
Yes.

Then that is the part that the authorities of the Department of, Railways and Canals are deepening to a depth of 22 feet. Perhaps the hon. minister; will explain why he has departed altogether from the recommendation of this commission, that he has appointed himself in reference to the erection of the elevators. If I understood the hon. minister rightly, he said that he was erecting elevators of a capacity of 2,000,000 bushels. The commission recommended that the two elevators be not constructed, that although there are foundations made for two of them only one should be constructed of 1,000,000 bushi els capacity. Why has the hon. minister departed from the recommendation of the commissioners in reference to that ?
On the ground of economy.
On the ground of economy when you are expending double the amount ?
Yes.

Has the hon. minister been listening? I say that the commission has recommended that only one elevator of a capacity of 1,000,000 bushels should be erected for the present, and if I understood the hon. minister rightly he is erecting two with a capacity of 2,000,000 bushels.
No, only one.
He said 2,000,000 bushels to the committee.

We are erecting one elevator of a capacity of 2,000,000 bushels. That seemed to be an economical course to pursue. The commissioners recommended two elevators, or rather they recommended one elevator to be commenced with a capacity of not less than 1,000,000 bushels, but having foundations to enable additional bins to be provided so that it would have a capacity within the near future of 2,000,000 bushels, and it certainly seemed to be in the interest of economy to simply build the one set of foundations now and erect an elevator Mr. EMMERSON.
capable of meeting all the natural requirements of the traffic that may he expected, within the next two or three years.

The Minister of Railways states what ? I understood him to state that he is erecting an elevator of a capacity of 2,000,000 bushels, having bins provided for use in case of emergency. The fact of the matter is that the commission have recommended only one elevator of a capacity of 1,000,000 bushels.
But that everything be done for an elevator of 2,000,000 bushels.

No, they did not do anything of the kind ; they state that foundations be prepared for two elevators, and that in the meantime only one be erected of a capacity of only 1,000,000 bushels. He is now erecting an elevator of a capacity of
2.000.	000 bushels.

I would like to know from the minister distinctly whether he is asking for an appropriation for an elevator of 1,000,000 capacity or more ? Is this for an elevator of 1,000,000 or 2,000,000 capacity ? He has been talking, and so has the Postmaster General, of an elevator of
2.000.	000 capacity. I would like to know which it is that is contemplated under this estimate.
I will repeat to my hon. friend that this appropriation is towards the construction of a 2;000,000-bushel elevator.
Has that been recommended ?
Yes, it has been recommended ; and it is recommended here.
Let us hear the words.

They recommend here :
That the work of putting in a suitable foundation and the erection of an elevator at Port Colborne Harbour to proceed with at once, the capacity to be not less than 1,000,000 bushels.
Hear, hear.

Certainly ; but the report does not say how much larger the elevator should be. It goes on and advises this :

and placed so that additional storage bins can be added when found necessary.
The capacity is evidently intended by the commissioners to be greater than 1,000,000 bushels ; it must not be less than 1,000,000 bushels. It does not confine it, as he says, indeed, It rather

Last year, in the discussion in this House, the present Minister of Railways and Canals told us that it was uncertain whether it was desirable to construct an elevator at all. It was then a

question with the minister whether an elevator should be constructed by the government or by private parties. To-day we are told that the minister has decided upon government construction of an elevator of 2,000,000 bushels capacity. For an hour before six o'clock, we got from the minister not one word of explanation as to why there should be an elevator at all. The first explanation we heard was from the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), who told us that some gentlemen, I think one was a Mr. Wolvin, had made application to the government for permission to construct an elevator as a private enterprise and some other gentlemen in Toronto, great capitalists, friends of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), had proposed a rival private enterprise.
They were all good Conservatives.
It does not matter in the expenditure of this money, I hope, whether they are Liberals or Conservatives.
Quite right.

I hope the Liberals will be all the more pleased if Conservatives spend the money. The hon. gentleman said that certain gentlemen in Toronto were rivals of Mr. Wolvin for the building of this elevator. We never heard a word of that when the minister asked us to vote this money. We were not informed that within the last twelve months there had been a solitary application to the government by any individual or company to construct an elevator ; not a word was uttered to us ; we were simply asked to vote this money for oue year's expenditure. We got the first intimation from the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), but having broken the, ice we heard something further from the minister, and he told us that nobody on either side of the House had heard a word of, that the Transportation Commissioners had reported upon this very subject. I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite, who, I think, owe a duty, every man of them, to their constituents and to the country, do they think it is right to sit behind the minister and blindly vote anything that is put in these estimates without inquiry ? I ask these gentlemen if they think that a million or so is nothing to this country, and that the criticism of these estimates should be left entirely to gentlemen on this side of the House ? Do they owe no duty to their constituents ? Have they no right to ask the minister why he asks $500,000 or $1,000,000 for a particular work ? Are they to sit mum, or say ' yea ' to everything that is put in these estimates 1 I hope not [DOT] I think that the criticism would come from these gentlemen far more effectively than from us. If one of these gentlemen should give utterance to his honest convictions on these subjects its influence
would be tenfold that of a criticism from this side of the House.
But I have been in this House for a few sessions, and I have yet to see one of these hon. members stand up and ask one question of the hon. gentlemen on the front benches as to why they propose any of these expenditures. Now, I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite. There are, I know, very many of them who sincerely desire to do what is in the country's interest. I ask these hon. gentlemen, why cannot they stand up in this House and ask the hon. gentlemen on the front benches, civilly, respectfully and humbly, why these moneys are to be expended. These hon. gentlemen may think that we are asking these questions with the sole object of opposing them. Let me tell them that there are gentlemen on this side of the House just as anxious, possibly far more anxious to see public money spent on the Welland canal than half the gentlemen who sit on the government benches, so long as it is spent reasonably and in the interest of the country. Why cannot hon. gentlemen opposite criticise the government in the same spirit ? When we know that a minister will listen respectfully and considerately to the representations of hon. gentlemen opposite, why cannot they use their influence reasonably and fairly, and criticise, not in a hostile spirit, but in a friendly spirit, every one of these items, and ask the government why they are spending a million when perhaps half a million would do ?

I have listened with some degree of interest to the lecture which has been read to us on this question by the hon. member for Hamilton. I doubt very much, however, if there is a stronger political partisan in parliament to-day than the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, or one who would allow his party leaders to pass items through parliament with less criticism than he would. We are quite prepared, Sir, to criticise every act of this government; I have criticised some of the acts of this government when I thought that criticism was justified. As I said this afternoon, it was a moot question whether or not this elevator at Port Colborne should be built by a private company or by the government. For myself, I thought at the time that it would be better for a private company to build it. I am not sure that I have changed that opinion yet. The government decided that it was wiser, in the interest of the country, that it should be built by the government, in view of the fact that no company would build it-and this, in my opinion, is the only consideration that would justify the government in building the elevator-without insisting on having a monopoly of the rights in the harbour.
Why so ?

Simply because it was a speculative affair. I know what I am

speaking about when I say that neither the Wolvin syndicate nor the Toronto gentlemen who formed themselves into a company for the purposes of transportation would consider the building of an elevator at Port Colborne and the putting on of a line of boats without having an absolute monopoly of the rights in the harbour I was not sure myself that it would not have been wise to have allowed the Canadian company-I would never have agreed to allow an American company-to have had the control of the situation. I do not know that the gentlemen who are interested in the company would object to my giving their names, as you can find them in the Act of incorporation : they are Frederick Nichols, William Mackenzie, I think Mr. W. R. Brock
all Canadians and men of means and enterprise who are willing to go into the work of developing the transportation facilities through our Canadian water routes ; but they would not undertake it without getting a monopoly of the rights at Port Colborne.
A monopoly of what rights ?

The rights for the construction of elevators on the two concrete piers which the government have constructed'for that purpose-not an absolute monopoly of all the rights in the harbour. No other company could have built elevators except at an enormous expense. The government built, with the approbation of parliament, these two concrete piers for the purpose of constructing elevators thereon, and they also built the breakwater which forms the harbour at Port Colborne. Prior to that there was no harbour there. Each of the two companies who were interested ill this matter told the government that they must have the exclusive right. The government refused to give the exclusive right to either company, and decided to build the elevator themselves.

They are on rock foundation. Now, the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) raised the Question this afternoon, whether or not the products of the Northwest can be carried to the seaboard cheaper by rail than by water. That is a question on which different people have different opinions.
Have you any doubt about it ?

I have no doubt that they can be taken to the seaboard cheaper by water than by rail ; but bon. gentlemen who are interested in railroad companies as the hon. member for West Toronto is, and as I understand the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is-
No, not a bit, and never was.

have an idea that the
products of the Northwest can be taken to the sea-board more cheaply by rail than by water. That was the basis of the argument of the hon. member for West Toronto this afternoon. There is one thing which has operated against the Welland canal. The action of the Grand Trunk Railway Company for years past has made it practically impossible to bring the products of the west through our water routes, by reason of the tact that the boats coming to Port Colborne had to lighter there before they could go thiough the canal. The quantity of grain they had to lighter at Port Colborne was so large that the freight upon it from Port Colborne to Port Dalhousie was such as to stop the traffic.
What did the piers cost ?

I have not got the figures The work was put up at public tender, and it has been carried on as all government work is ; and I might say further that, much against my will, the contract was given to a good thorough Conservative.

That is not the point. The point I wish to make is that the cost of constructing these concrete piers was not a difficulty in the way of a company establishing a transportation system and building piers for themselves. I understand that the piers cost only about $10,000.
I am not sure what the piers cost.
Are the piers on a solid foundation or on piles ?

That has been going on for years and is the reason why the grain cannot be taken through the Welland canal. Now the idea is to have an elevator at Port Colborne and tranship from the big upper lake boats, carrying 250,000 bushels of wheat, into it, and thence into canal sized boats carrying 75,000 bushels to Montreal and Quebec. That is the proposition. Our canals have been bunt at an enormous expense. What are we to do with them ? I heard the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair) say in this House that he believed it would be an excellent thing for this country to have canals even if nothing were taken through them, because they would be a regulator of freight rates.
Hear, hear.

But we cannot regulate Ine freight rates by means of our canals unless we have some system of transhipping our grain at Port Colborne. It has been said that the Georgian bay route, the Ottawa canal route, is a better route. That may be. That is a matter for discussion, but we have got the Welland canal route, we have built the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence canals. Are we to utilize them

or let them fall into decay and become useless ?
That is the question.

That is the whole question. My hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) asked why not, instead of building an elevator at Port Colborne, take your boats to Buffalo and take the grain at Buffalo. But I ask him in reply, does he want to build up Buffalo at the expense of our Canadian towns and water routes ? And when the grain gets to Buffalo, it will go from there by railway or by the Erie canal to the sea-board. It will not be possible to get it back again. The only way we can get through our Canadian waterways the grain products of the Northwest at present, is to have an elevator at Port Colborne into which these large upper lake boats can unload, and from which that grain can be transhipped into canal sized boats which will carry it to the sea-board. And in this way the grain can be carried cheaper to the sea-board than by taking it to Buffalo and transhipping it from there through American routes. That is demonstrated absolutely. The hon. member for West Toronto, (Mr. Osier) said this afternoon that the season was so short, our canal system being closed up in November or early in December, that we could not compete with the American routes. But what is the United States government doing ? Notwithstanding the opportunities for transportation which they have from Buffalo to New York and Boston and the different places to which they send these products, they have made an appropriation of $100,000,000 to enlarge the Erie canal.
The New York state government has.
Yes, the New York state government has made an appropriation of $100,000,000 to enlarge the Erie canal, and the Erie canal is closed up two or three weeks earlier than the Welland canal.
That is the local government.

It is the government of the state of New York. 1 cannot quite understand why the hon. gentleman should lay so much stress on this. I do not see how it can make any possible difference. It is the government of the wealthiest state in the United States, and the people of that state who, I suppose, have an idea of the fitness of things, believe that the expenditure of this money will be beneficial to that state and the public generally. In any case that is what they are doing. And all that this government asks is that, after having spent all the money we have done in connection with our waterways, we should now simply put the keystone in the
arch and do what must necessarily be done in order to give us a complete transportation system. All the government asks i$ that we should build an elevator at Port Colborne, which must be done unless we intend deepening the Welland canal to 22 feet. But no one, at present at any rate, would support any such proposition. No one would think of deepening the Welland] canal, at present at any rate, to 22 feet. But if you build an elevator at Port Col-, borne, whether it be a one million or two million bushel elevator, you must build one that will supply what is required. A two million elevator can be built for about one-third cheaper than you could build two elevators of the capacity of a million bushels each, so that the government will be saving money by building one large elevator instead of two small ones. And I firmly believe that in the near future another elevator of two million bushels capacity will be needed at Port Colborne. I am inclined to think that under private enterprise that, condition of affairs might be more quickly realized ; but I am satisfied with what the government is doing, because I believe most firmly that what it proposes to do will bring about the transportation of the products of our great Northwest through our Canadian channels at the cheapest possible rates. And if that can be accomplished, surely no one can criticise severely, if at all, this proposed expenditure.

I am gratified at the remarks of my hon. friend because in fact they support the theory which I have always thought should guide us in the erection of elevators. He says that there were applications from two companies for the erection of elevators at this particular station, but that neither of them would undertake the work unless they were given exclusive privileges. But when questioned as to the exclusive privileges which they asked, it appears that all they wanted was the right to erect these elevators on the two foundations which the 'government are putting in. Was there any other exclusive tights that they asked for ? None. All the exclusive rights which these private individuals wanted was the right to use the foundations which the government are putting in for the purpose of erecting elevators at a cost of some $20,000 or $30,000 a piece. The hon. gentleman has a leaning towards the argument which I made in the former part of the evening, and I have no doiibt that he is convinced from the bottom of his soul that the policy of the government is a wrong one. Application was made by these companies, not only to erect elevators, but also to build steamboats for the purpose of utilizing the facilities which the government have provided by the deepening of the harbour. They were to have no exclusive privileges beyond the right of erecting eleva-

tors on the foundations built by the government. The whole of the harbour of Port Col-borne was open to any other private individuals who desired to j;rect elevators if they would, but on their own foundations. X need not appeal to my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) because he is too intelligent not to know that an elevator owned by private individuals, who have their connections by boats and who could put on a line of steamers to the upper lakes, would be far more profitable than a government owned elevator. Private enterprise will succeed where a government will fail. Fancy a lot of government officials running an elevator, who do not care two cents whether a bushel of grain went into the elevator or not from one end of the year to the other. But in what a different position would be private enterprise. These people would embark their own money in the scheme, and in order to get a return from their investment, they must have transportation facilities and connections. They would build up large boats which would carry the grain most economically to Port Colborne. But, when we inquire into it, they have no exclusive privilege except, as my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) has stated, the privilege of erecting an elevator upon foundations which the government built because they could build them more cheaply in connection with the other works. What right has the government to enter upon business which should be left to private enterprise ? What right have they to provide facilities for transporting grain, if those facilities can be provided by private enterprise ? Any person who knows anything of government undertakings of this kind, knows that they cannot successfully compete with undertakings directed by private enterprise. X need not enter upon that question now, nor need I ask the Minister of Railways whether he thinks that government railways can be managed as economically as railways that are privately owned. This domain of private business is one upon which the government has no right to enter. What right have they to go into the elevator business ? None whatever. This fostering of industries of this kind seems peculiar to this government. The hon. gentleman objects because my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) advocates the government ownership of railways and of telegraph and telephone lines. There are some public utilities that are peculiarly within the province of government. One of these is the post office and, as a legitimate part of it, the telegraph and telephone services. The question of the public ownership of railways may become a question for the people of this country to decide. But, even if the government owned the elevator, could not they lease it to a private individual to carry on business in connection with grain transportation, and
impose upon the lessee conditions necessary to protect the public interest ? In the world of private enterprise the interests of the public are protected by competition, and there is no business in which competition is keener than in the transportation of grain from the upper lake ports. The government have a commission to inquire into this business of transportation. That commission reports that certain facilities should be provided. But the Minister of Railways doubles the recommendation of the commissioners.
Oh, no.
The commission recommends an elevator of
Not less than a million bushels.
And the hon. gentleman draws the inference that that is justification for elevator capacity of a hundred million bushels.
Only two millions.

If a recommendation of a million is justification for providing two millions, why should it not be made justification for a hundred millions ? Mr. Chairman, this question of transportation is a nice question. It is too late to discuss it fully to-night. But, though the question is so great a one, and though this expenditure at Port Colborne is so large, we have nothing from the minister to show that that expenditure is justified. The expenditure of the elevator will be about $1,000,000, is it not ?
I stated the amount-including the foundation, $1,100,000.
The deepening of the channel from the entrance locks to Port Colborne will cost $500,000 or $600,000 more
That would have to be done any way.

The question of this elevator at Port Colborne can only be discussed in reference to the whole project. The expenditure for deepening Port Colborne and providing the second breakwater -the one additional to that already under construction-will be in the neighbourhood of $2,500,000. So you have here an expenditure of at least $4,000,000. The government must not find fault if we want the fullest information on the subject, or if we criticise that expenditure. We have been unable to get from the minister a single statement as to the commercial benefit to the Dominion to follow the development of the traffic of that port. I am not discussing particularly the question whether branches of the Trent Valley canal should or should not be extended to Schomberg and Aurora. I have the habit-I wish the Postmaster General had the same habit-of not talking of a matter until I know something about it. Now I will talk of a matter that the Postmaster General cannot deny. I am sorry he does not appreciate the situation better than he appears to ; he seems to be | oblivious of the fact that it is a very grave offence, a very grave indiscretion in any member of parliament, and particularly a prominent member of a government, to go into a riding, particularly in his own riding, on the eve of a general election, when votes are to be won, and ought to be won by honest means, and there to hold out a bait to the people to vote for him. It is not a question of the policy of constructing the canal. When that matter has been laid before parliament, when this large scheme that has been foreshadowed by the speech from the Throne, it is quite time enough for any member of the government to go before the people and announce that he is in favour of the scheme. I venture to say, although a young man, a young member of parliament, that it is not becoming in a member of a cabinet, without consultation witli his associates, without the scheme having been officially before the cabinet council for consideration, to pledge himself in his own riding to promote a scheme, whether it is or is not supposed to be in the interest of his constituents. How stands the Postmaster General in regard to this matter? He stands as a pledged man, bound and shackled in regard to this proposition. He is not a free man to sit as a cabinet minister when that delegation comes here, and to give a judicial consideration to the question. No, he is one of the promoters, as it is stated here, he is one of those who advocated the scheme, he is one of the active men who initiated it, and therefore he cannot represent the people of Canada in this matter. He is a shackled man before this delegation comes to Ottawa to consult with the government. But the Postmaster General is not in an unique position. He talked about unique positions a little

while ago, but he is not alone in failing to grasp the niceties which surround the actions of cabinet ministers. He is on a par with the unfortunate position in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce stood a few months ago when, in discussing the Jackson transaction, he failed to see what was the real issue before the House, and ventured to condone an offence without realizing the enormity of the offence. So it is with the Postmaster General to-night. 1 regret it exceedingly, I regret it because of its effect on public life in Canada, I regret it as a Canadian on behalf of the people of this country, that a cabinet minister, a gentleman not new to the position, one who has been long in office, does not see the gravity of the offence he committed when he became a party to the promotion of a scheme which had never been foreshadowed even by the speech from the Throne.

I desire to say a word or two in answer to the stand the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) has taken here to-night. He has robed himself in righteousness and made broad his phylacteries like the Pharisees of old. thanking God he is not like other men. He reads a lecture to the members of this House on honesty, integrity and straightforwardness. We had the spectacle last year, on the last day of the last session of the last parliament, of this self same hon. gentleman getting up on the floor of this House and attempting to besmirch the name of a member of parliament ; and to prove his statement he read a letter, and in reading that letter he purposely left out a sentence, he purposely suppressed a sentence in that letter which turned the whole force of the argument against himself, and left him with not a leg to stand on. That is the hon. gentleman uho gets up now, X would like to call him my cacological friend, and attempts to read us a lesson. He should be the last man to do a thing like that. A gentleman who committed a wrong like that last session has no right to get up and read a lecture to this House on honesty. It ill becomes the hon. gentleman to make a statement like that unless he is prepared to stand by every one of his actions, let alone his words.

Somebody asks me to attend to this hon. gentleman. I do not think I will. There are a number 'of hon. gentlemen in this House who know exactly what the hon. gentleman is referring to, and it is not surprising to me that he feels sore. The hon. gentleman on that occasion had to admit-and I can furnish the ' Hansard ' with the whole discussion-be had to admit that he had been guilty of making statements which did not sound well in the mouth of any hon. gentleman or any member of this House, statements that were made far away from this House, out in British Columbia, statements that I read from 42}
papers furnished to me. It is right and fitting that this hon. gentleman should come to the rescue of the Postmaster General. If not a case of birds of a feather flocking together, it is a case of returning a service where the Postmaster General came to his rescue on that occasion. I told the hon. member that as certain papers had been placed in my hands of which I knew nothing at all about
Nothing at all ?

Yes, of which I knew nothing at all-hon. gentlemen had better not shout until they are out of the bush-papers of which I knew nothing at all had _ been placed in my hands to bring before the House, and I took occasion to tell the hon. gentleman that I would endeavour to bring them up at a time that was convenient to him. I had waited for some time-I think he was at Montreal-for him to return. We were friendly. I could not get an opportunity when the hon. gentleman was present until the last day of the session. The Postmaster General, acting on behalf of my hon. friend, came over to me and seeing that I had a bundle of papers before me said, I hope you are not going to read all those papers because the time is short. He said the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Macpherson) wanted to leave soon on the train. I said, well, there are certain portions that I will read, and I went on to show the Postmaster General what I proposed to read. Well, he says, cut it short, just give a part of it, don't take up much time ; and so I promised him I would shorten it as much as I could.
I was not particularly familiar with the papers. They had been marked before they had been placed in my hands. I read such portions as I thought would be necessary, but not all that would be necessary if I had had more time at my disposal. These papers were in the hands of the hon. minister, and every one of the letters which I read was in the possession of the government, and was known to be in the possession of the government, for weeks before the discussion came on. It was not essential or reasonable that I should read the whole of the letters. Subsequently, the hon. acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman), whom I see in the House, got up and. taking some of the papers I had handed over, said that I had left out a sentence in a letter that would have qualified what I had read.
I was not professing to read the whole letter. He quoted it, and I said that I had not read such a letter,, and neither I had, according to the bundle in my hand and probably according to the papers in his hand. But the hon. gentleman who has just spoken says that I wilfully and deliberately suppresed a portion of a letter, that I did not make it as full as I ought to have made it. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Macpherson), who has interjected something irrelevant in

the discussion, will receive attention at my hands on some occasion when the House is not so busy-in the dog days, in the good old summer time to come, perhaps; but I do not intend to pay much attention to him now. I am ready to refer to ' Hansard ' and to deal with the whole question, and if he; goes much farther, I will be liable to ask him certain questions that he will not like to answer. But I am not going to depart from the subject we have in hand now. It is quite right that he should come to the rescue of the hon. Postmaster General, and if there is any one who should apologize, it is the hon. Postmaster General, whom I endeavoured to accommodate.

I ask no man to apologize for me, and at any time the hon. gentleman wishes to follow up that line of attack upon me, he will find me doing business at the old stand. I want to say further when the hon. gentleman says here that I was obliged to retract something I said, he cannot find on the pages of the revised or unrevised ' Hansard ' anything to show that I was obliged to retract one solitary word.

It is not remarkable that) the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macplierson) should be inexact as to what occurred many months or a year ago, when he cannot remember what was said two minutes ago. I did not say that he was obliged to retract anything, but I said he was obliged to admit certain statements, which he made at Vancouver, and which were read by me, to be true. That is all. The hon. gentleman says I can commence the discussion of the matter at any time I see fit. I am not going to do anything of the kind. The time of this House is too valuable for me to waste it in dealing with the hon. gentleman who has just spoken.

The hon. gentleman is very funny. He tries to get away from the point. Does the hon. gentleman deny, as it is stated in the paper, that he was present at the meeting and spoke in favour of the scheme ? I read it, not only in this paper, but I read it in other papers, amongst them the Newmarket ' Era,' I think. While I was travelling on the train I met a gentleman who had just come from the meeting. I know it was discussed broadcast throughout the last general election, and I am calling attention to it here because I think it does not become a cabinet minister, on the eve of an election, to make promises to the electors which may influence their votes.

An abstract declaration of principle may be a very good thing. I attended the meeting in question, I addressed myself to the meeting as other citizens did, and I was saying what I am saying now, that the district would be advantaged by the construction of such a work, but the question of its cost and the question of its feasibility were matters entirely in the future, and the determination of the work must depend upon these considerations. That is my view to-day. I hope the result of the inquiry will show that the work is feasible, and that the prices come within a reasonable figure or as reasonable as will commend itself to support at the hands of this House.
Is it a fact that engineers or surveyors were put on ?

When we come to discuss that question, the way it happened to come up at that time will be made quite clear. It grew out of the decision of the Railway Commission seriously affecting a great enterprise in our district. The people were seriously intending to move away -because of the railway freight rates. The matter came up in that way, and the people of our district were extremely uneasy lest this large enterprise should move away on account of the rates of freight charged by the Grand Trunk Railway Company on the commodities used and exported by that enterprise.
The hon. gentleman has not answered me, but probably he will tell me now ?
About the engineers ?
Yes.
The engineers have been in the field ever since, and I think they are in the field yet.
I do not want to prolong this matter ; if the hon. gentleman will tell me now, that is an end of it-what large enterprise was it that was about to leave ?
Messrs. Kane & Sons.
Of Newmarket ?
Of Newmarket.
Yes, the gentleman who is named in this paper as the promoter of this scheme.
He is one of the firm.
By what authority were these engineers sent into the field ?
By the authority of the Minister of Railways.

I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals whether there has been any money spent on this work of building the elevators during] the present year ? There was money voted for it, but was there any money spent, and when ' was the scheme undertaken by the government of building this elevator ?

The matter was under consideration last May after the report of the Transportation Commission and during the summer. I asked parliament at the last session to make an appropriation of $400,000. Arrangements were then made with a view to having plans made for the foundations, and tenders were asked for. Arrangements were also made for the making of plans and specifications for the superstructure. The contract has been let for the substructure but the plans are not quite complete for the superstructure. I hope they will be ready within a week or two and then tenders will be called for.

As the $400,000 was ill the main estimates last year, which were published before the date of the Transportation Commission's report, the government's decision must have been reached before the report was received V
The $400,000 was not in the main estimates but in the supplemen-taries which came down in August.
This seems to me to be exactly the same scheme as that which was outlined by the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) and which he pressed on the attention of the House.
I do not know what he did.

His contention was that it was a scheme that should be undertaken by the government, and he urged it on the ground that the storage of grain there ought to be made as cheap as possible, and that for that reason it should be kept in the hands of the government, for on that would largely depend the possibility or the probability of a large amount of grain passing by that route. This is exactly the same scheme and therefore must have been undertaken before the Transportation Commission reported on it. Speaking of this report it seems to me that for a great commission, a commission supposed to be composed of able men, this was about .tlie most superficial report on the transportation question, so far as that locality is concerned, thai I ever saw. It does not pretend to say that another bushel of grain will be taken down the St. Lawrence on account of it or that a bushel will be diverted from the Erie canal. The commission simply seems to recommend what the government had already cfiscussed and agreed upon so that the government might be fortified in the policy to which they had practically committed themselves over a year before. If that is all the great Transportation Commission can do we had better avoid the expense of keeping that commission going in the future.

The report of the Transportation Commission is certainly brief, but it states facts ; it does not indulge in any prophetic visions or fancy flights but states facts as to the conditions which prevail there and points out why it is necessary to have an elevator built in order to utilize and develop to their full capacity the works which have been constructed at great cost to the country in connection with the canal. 1 do not know anything about any views which Mr. Tarte entertained ; I only know that after this report came in I brought the matter, in a report to council, to the consideration of my colleagues and that it was discussed during the summer. The item was finally put in the estimates to the extent of $400,000 with a view to carrying out the policy which is outlined in the report referred to. It has no connection beyond that with any views which might have been entertained by other gentlemen. There may have been those who entertained these views; I have no doubt there are because they seem to be wise conclusions and 1 trust that the good judgment of the people of this country and of the business interests of the country will concur in their conclusion and will approve of the action of parliament in making an appropriation.

The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) gave us to understand that there were two corporations prepared to build this elevator, and not only 1 to do that but to build boats suitable to pass

through tlie canal and handle the grain. We have heard a good deal of argument with reference to the possibility of the government building an elevator. As a business proposition we would readily understand that the men who are. building the elevator would be willing and ready at least to build boats to carry the grain both from Port Arthur to Port Colborne and from Port Colborne to Montreal. I would like to have the minister explain at least part of the arrangement into which these companies were willing to enter.

Propositions did come to the department that were sent there by the member for Welland (Mr. German). He has very correctly stated that in view of the policy outlined by the Transportation Commission they were not entertained or taken into consideration. I think that in a general way they wished the government to construct the foundations and to give them the privilege of building elevators on the pier after it had been constructed, the company then to have the exclusive control of these elevators in connection with their transportation lines. The propositions were not taken into serious consideration for the reason that they seemed to be opposed to the best interests of the country, that it would be creating a monopoly in connection with the traffic whatever it might amount to and would not inure to the advantage either of the business interests of the country or of the canal.

This elevator, I understand, is to contain not less than 2,000,000 bushels. Is it believed that there will be any great advantage in having a 2,000,000 bushel elevator there for the storage of grain at the close of the year. An elevator of the capacity of 2,000,000 bushels would be much better than an elevator of the capacity of 1,000,000. What object is there in putting in a large quantity of grain when navigation has closed.

In the first instance, the class of vessels that will furnish the products of the west to that elevator will be a large class, and those products will necessarily be transhipped in smaller vessels suitable to the canal navigation. It will be necessary to have an elevator of large storage capacity, because the incoming freight will be greater than the outgoing at particular times during the season of navigation. More than that as is outlined in the report of the commissioners, railway connection should be had with the elevator,! nud the grain that would not be taken through the canal, by reason of the closing of navigation, could 'be stored at the elevator and taken out from time to time by railway transportation. The commissioners recommend an elevator of not less capacity1 than one million bushels ; but they contemplate another elevator, because they say, prepare your foundation and have every-Mr. ARMSTRONG.
thing in readiness for even more than that* 'I he capacity of the elevator, in their judgment, must not be less than one million bushels, but they do not coniine it to that) capacity. One elevator of two million bushels capacity can be constructed for almost) a third less-so I am advised by a very competent engineer-than two elevators of one million bushels capacity each. Therefore) having in mind the almost certainty of requiring two one million bushel elevators within the very near future, it seemed to bs the interest of economy that one of the larger capacity should be built, especially as if could also be operated at much less ex* pense. One power of larger capacity could be utilized in connection with the two million elevator much more cheaply than could two powers for isolated plants in separate elevators of one million capacity each. There would also be a smaller number of employees iand officials. These are the reasons which led me, upon whom some responsibility rested in connection with the matter, to recommend to my colleagues the construction of one elevator of two million bushels capacity.

It does not seem to me tluu the reasons given are very strong. The principal one is that the grain might be stored there, and might be moved by railway after navigation closed. Is it likely that the grain would go such a long way roupd to be moved by railway when it could: go to Midland or Parry Sound? Not very likely. There is a reason to my mind why there might be a large elevator, that is, to store the large quantity of Manitoba wheat that is used in the Ontario mills in the winter time. With regard to the necessity of having a large elevator so that it would not get filled up during navigation, I am satisfied that if you had a million bushel elevator, there would be plenty of craft to take all the grain that reached it during the season of navigation. I would not think it likely that there would be a great blockade of grain there after navigation opened. But after navigation closed, it might be advisable to have more storage capacity, not for the purpose of having the grain taken to Montreal by rail, but for the purpose of having it there for distribution to the mills ini the province of Ontario in the winter time to be mixed with Ontario wheat. That .is the strongest argument that could be advanced, in myjudgment, for a large elevator. But the feature of the Transportation Commission that attracted my attention was this. The great object of the large expenditure at Port Colborne, as stated by the exMinister of rublic Works, was the desirability of diverting to the St. Lawrence routs the grain which goes from Chicago and Duluth via the Erie canal to New York. That, and that alone, must be the justification of this expenditure which when completed will be over $4,000,000. But this Transportation

Commission seems to have completely ignored that in their interim report, on which the hon. minister is acting in making this large expenditure, for they are silent on that point.

There was one observation made by the minister a few minutes ago which seems to me to emphasize the objection raised by the hon. member from' South Lanark to the government entering into this business which ought to be com ducted by private enterprise. The hon. gen-i tieman says' that the wheat will arrive at this elevator, will go into it, and will be subsequently forwarded, perhaps by rail, perhaps at the conclusion of the winter season by vessels. Has the hon gentleman reflected for a moment that that involves the government entering into a warehouse business ? If you receive consignments of wheat of different classes and grades and from various persons you will have to issite warehouse receipts. These will be handled by banks, large advances will be made upon them, pommercial transactions will occur, and all* in reliance upon documents issued by an agent of the government. I think it is a most serious question. Have the government considered it as it ought to be considered ? You are going to have perhaps two mililon bushels of wheat in your elevators at the end of the season. That wheat will be held on behalf of various companies, commission merchants, railways, ships and other interests.
A certificate from the government as to any quantity held in store will be commercial paper, negotiable in the banks, upon which enormous sums of money will be advanced. The government will be responsible for the documents issued by their agents ; and one of the most difficult matters to be conducted by any commercial body will be conducted by a few government appointees who were never brought up to the business and know little or nothing about it. I have had some experience myself of the difficulty of conducting an elevator business. There is no line of business in which the persons or_ company responsible run more risk than "in this particular business which the government are proposing to enter into. I am inclined to think that a hasty conclusion has been arrived at and that the government have not fully considered what the construction and management of this elevator will lead them to. It may be that the government are under the impression that they will build an elevator and then perhaps turn it over to somebody else, but we have not had a word to that effect from the minister. So far as we know, the government propose to become warehousemen. They propose to enter into the commercial business of issuing warehouse receipts and conducting all the enormous transactions involved in the business including the liability to banks, endorsers and tranferees. And all these various ramifications are to be conducted by some gentlemen of the civil service who have had no training in anything of the kind. The whole of this discussion from first to last shows that there has not been given to this subject the careful consideration that it ought to have received. For an hour the minister did not tell us one word as to the grounds on which he was acting. It was not until the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) told us about the proposition of a couple of private enterprises to build the elevators that we knew anything about that offer. And it was only after we got that information that (he Postmaster General told us about the report from the transportation committee.
I told you about that before the Postmaster General spoke at all-I read extracts from it.
If the hon. gentleman did, it certainly escaped my observation.
The Postmaster General made no reference to it whatever.

I may perhaps be wrong in that respect, but I say it was not until after the hon. member for Welland told us about the proposition from two private companies that we knew that any such proposition had been made or that we heard a word about the report of the Transportation Commission. It was only then, for the first time, that we heard that the subject had been reported upon by that commission. We have never seen that report. It has never been laid on the table. We never heard until to-night that offers had been made by any parties to construct these elevators, and we are asked to grant millions of money without giving the matter as much consideration as a business man would give to an expenditure of $500.
May I ask the hon. minister if the erection of an elevator by the government will prevent any private company from constructing an elevator in that harbour ?
The government may prevent any other elevator being built on their concrete piers. I question whether there would be room for another on these piers.
Would there not be room for 200 elevators in the harbour ?

It is not merely the elevators but the slips in connection with the elevators which must be considered. There are quite a number of vessels prying over the lakes which will require to utilize the elevators and *will require advantages in connection with the unloading.

The hon. gentleman says there is only room for two elevators. I asked him what is the distance from the entrance lock to the harbour and he said 4,050 feet.

Could you not put an elevator along the whole length of the canal from the entrance and the lock of the harbour ?
I am speaking of the two concrete foundations. You can build elevators away down at the mouth and there is no reason why you could not.

My hon. friend
means that you can only put two elevators on the foundations for two. [DOT]
What I ask is that supposing private corporations wanted the privilege of erecting elevators would that be granted them or is it the policy of the government to monopolize the elevator business.

That point has not been considered in the concrete form in which my hon. friend puts it, but I am satisfied that if any private corporation wanted to build a elevator, it would be open to them to do it, on such conditions as the government might see fit to impose.

I was very sorry to find that on a question such as this a minister of the Crown or anybody else could drift away into ancient politics and go back (to the expenditure on the Welland canal in generations gone by and ask who was responsible for it. What is the use, in this day and generation, of going away back to make political capital out of the expenditure on canals, which were built under conditions which the most of us to-day know nothing about. What struck me in connection with this discussion as to the relative advantage of government ownership and the building of these elevators by private enterprise, is this : If the government build the elevators and these large vessels unload into them, where are they going to get the barges into which to tranship that grain ? But if a company should build these elevators, they would do so for the purpose of making money and would no doubt build the barges required to take the grain down the canal.
They would build an elevator for coni! mercial reasons-to make money. Having built the elevator, would that company also be in a position to build vessels of proper capacity for the canal to carry the grain from the elevator down to the shipping port at Montreal, Quebec, or wherever they *wished to go ? The hon. minister told us, with a great flourish of trumpets, about the number of vessels upon the upper lakes that would come down to Port Oolborne. I admire his faith in the development of the country, for I am a Canadian also. But, even if there are so many vessels as he says on the upper lakes, surely three or four of these vessels would carry enough to fill hisi elevator, and then where would he be if barges -were not provided to take the grain away ? Why, the whole traffic would be blocked. We may talk as much as we like, but we should not go beyond the bounds of

common sense in dealing with this plain practical matter. It is too big and too serious a question to have our minds distracted by party politics when we are trying to deal with it. As a practical matter, I would ask how much of the grain that reaches Buffalo is ultimately exported from the United States. I have not the figures before me, and at my time of life I cannot carry these figures in my mind ; but I understand that a very small proportion of the grain that goes through the elevators at Buffalo is exported to foreign countries. If that is the fact, will the minister explain to me how he can possibly hope to divert any part of that traffic from Buffalo to Port Col-borne ? To say that this could be done' would be the most absurd proposition that could be made. All he can hope to secure will be a share of the grain that goe^ through Buffalo for export to foreign countries. The report that the minister has read is not complete for our purpose. It does not) go into figures, and so does not give us the information upon which to base an intelligent judgment with regard to this vote. I hardly like to venture to give advice to the minister, but I must say, whether they like it or not, that I have found a lack of readiness on their part to give this committee information that it ought to have. The Minister of Railways has read the report of the commission, not when he introduced the resolution, but, apparently-I hope he will excuse me if I am wrong-when it was dragged out of him and he could not help himself.

The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) spoke of two other offers made to build an elevator at this point. It would not have been amiss for the minister to bring down information concerning these. We have an extract from the report of the Transportation Commission, but we should have the other too. It may not) prove valuable information, but I think it would be better if we had it before disposing of this item finally.

I am quite ready to bring down any desired information, but I feel sure hon. gentlemen opposite will not seek to have the item stand over on that account. We have discussed this matter exhaustively. No item has been passed, and I think we ought to make some progress.
I would like to go on with other items. IJ have already agreed with some hon. gentlemen opposite to allow some of the items to stand because some gentlemen on the other side who wish to discuss them could not be present this evening. Therefore, I would like to get this item through. The report of the Transportation Commission was referred to by me and I read an extract from it that I happened to have. I did not know at the time that a copy of the full report was in the House. But again after I sat down, and the discussion proceeded, the chief engi-

neer told me he had a copy of the report here, and 1 brought it to the notice of the committee. I did so at the first opportunity. Hon. gentlemen opposite and on this side also wished to speak and I bided my time. It certainly would be an advantage to this vote, as hon. gentlemen opposite will admitl to have that report before the committee, and had I known that a copy of it was here,
I would have read the whole report. The extract that I did read, I read at the outset of my remarks in explanation of the vote.

My recollection is that at that time the decision had not been reached in the matter. The subject was under discussion in May, when I brought to the notice! of my colleagues by the way of report, the contents of the report of the Transportation 'Commission. The matter was not finally settled even at the time the House was asked for the vote.

But let me read to the minister his own statement to the House on the 3rd of August, 1904, as reported in ' Hansard ' of that year, page 8380 :
It occurred to me that the elevators might be free even if the canals were not. But I would naturally expect that the public who use these elevators should pay for them. It is a question of policy as to whether a private corporation should have the right to build an elevator or whether it would be better for the government to do it.
The policy adopted is that the government shall do it, there being so many different shippers whose interests might clash. Therefore, the government would charge the ordinary elevator dues. That would be my idea.
Then it was settled at that time. Without referring to the record, I was under the impression that ib had not been settled at that time. But ib is only a question of date.

That is the all important question before the committee, and I do not wonder at my hon. friend from Northumber-j land calling the attention of the government to the fact that they are unwilling at times to give us information. Here is the fact that an important transportation commis-l sion had already reported last year, the report being in the hands of the government, and still the government have allowed this matter to come up involving the expenditure of nearly $3,000,000, as stated at that timej
to build a 2,000,000 bushel elevator. They a'lowed the committee to go on and discuss that, and all the time they withheld from the committee the report of the Transportation Commission.

There was no object in withholding it. I have already stated i that I was under the impression that that report had been presented to parliament, as indeed the interim report with regard to the ; St. John harbour had been presented to parliament. Until the question arose here tonight I certainly had no idea, but that it was within the knowledge of the House.
My hon. friend does not pretend to say now that he was of the opinion that the committee had this report in their possession last year.
Yes.
I am amazed at that statement. because this question was up then. Was it printed and distributed to the members ? No more important document could be printed.
I thought it had been placed before the House with the report concerning the St. John harbour.

I accept the hon. gentleman's statement when he says he understood the committee had it in tlieir possession. But the fact remains that the minister allowed this discussion to take place last year, involving an enormous expenditure, and he did not give the committee the report of the Transportation Commission, nor did he give it to the House at the beginning of this session. This item was up for discussion last evening, and still there was no mention of the report.

I wish to say a word with regard to the suggestion of the minister that we allow this item to pass, because wo have been discussing it for some time, and he has no objection to bring down these offers later on. There is this inconvenience about it, that after we have voted the money it cannot be of the same interest to us. it is before we vote the money that we require the information to enable us to judge whether we are going right. I have no desire to obstruct the passage of the vote, at the same time I think we ought to see those offers before we dispose of the item. We desire the information so that we may act intelligently.

They cannot affect the question materially. I acknowledge that the House should have these offers, but they do not bear materially on the question of this vote. It must be borne in mind that parliament is already committed to this work. There is no departure from the policy of the government constructing the elevator, This parliament committed itself a year ago

to a policy of that kind, and authorized the mation that I speak of it at the present government to expend $100,000.	time.
And that without the information which was in the government's possession.

Parliament was evidently satisfied with the information it had at that time. There was no reason why hon. members should not have had it. I couldi have no interest in withholding it, as it is information that entirely supports the proposition made by the government. But parliament having committed itself to tlm principle of constructing an elevator at that point, and placed at the disposal of the government $400,000, it seems to me that my hon. friend, in asking the matter to stand over now, is not serving the purpose that he desires to serve. Hon. gentlemen whoi were here last session will bear witness that whenever I promised to bring down infort mation, that promise was fulfilled as early as -possible. 1 can promise my hon. friend that the information he requires will be furnished on Monday.

The minister says that the House committed itself to this expenditure last year, and that it did so without information. But last year we were confronted with two dilemmas. We made an effort to get information and we could not, and were obliged to let many items go through without information. First there was put up a plea that the minister was a new minister and therefore was not familiar with the business, and out of charity wo had to let him pass over many things without the explanations we would have exacted from an older minister. Moreover, we| never knew when there was any information in the possession of a minister. I am not applying that remark to the present minister, because he is better than some of them ; but we never knew whether the information was in possession of a minister and he was so obstinate that he would not give it, or whether he had not the information, and in many cases we were obliged to go blindly. Does he not see that if we did what he desires us to do, that if wa should let it go without this information, we would be practically repeating the same blunder that we have committed in Other instances. -Suppose, for instance, that these two offers were much more favourable than we might reasonably anticipate they were,' we have not that knowledge because the information has not been given to the committee. We have voted about $400,000 and we are asked to vote $310,000, because wei have committed ourselves to it already, but, we are just adding to it. We are increasing the degree without increasing the intelligence with which we are doing it and it is on account of the absence of that infor-

I would like to draw the attention of the committee to the statement of the hon. minister just to show how absurd his proposition is. He says that he very generously gave us the information when we asked for it. We did not know anything about this report being in his possession. Here is a commission that we were paying, and the members of which are the servants of the people, but I think the trouble arose largely from the fact that the present ministers think they are czars, and that they are not the servants of the people. Here is a commission that the people are paying, obtaining information that an humble member of the House of Commons like myself cannot obtain. If the hon. minister! will consult his deputy when I conclude the few remarks which I propose to make, I will) be very much obliged to him. If he were as anxious to get information -when he was out of the House as he is in the House, we would not have all this trouble in getting information from him. What reason has the hon. minister for having a report in his possession that is made to him in his capacity as minister when he has not thought it necessary to have it printed and given to the public, so that the public might understand what that commission has been doing in the interest of the people who are paying for it ? He tells us very blandly, and with that generous smile he puts on
It is not put on. It is natural. Do not be unkind.

It is not put on ? I thought it was, because it is so bland that a wayfaring man, even a fool, might read that it is deceptive. If the hon. minister upon getting that report had printed it, we would have known what it contained. I fancy the trouble is that the hon. minister -I do not blame him and I do not criticise him more than I do other ministers-fails to get any information in reference to the .estimates until he comes down to the House and asks the committee to vote them. Then he has to talk to his deputy and get the information that he should have in his hands when he comes before the House, instead of having to refer to his deputy or some one else to ascertain whether the criticism made of his estimates by some hon. member is well founded or not. A minister of the Crown is the servant of the people just as I am. We are paying him for his services as a minister. We paid that commission to give us certain information which they gave to the minister, and from the fact that he neglected his duty by failing to have that report printed and put in the hands of the committee, we have had three or four hours of discussion-useless discussion, perhaps. There is the whole trouble in a nut shell, and if ministers only realized that they were delaying their own estimates by

their-I was going to say ignorance, but I will not use that word-but from the fact that they do not post themselves in connection with their estimates, thus causing the country to expend a lot of money for useless talk, I am sure they would make an effort to prepare themselves more thoroughly. If they would get that information and give it to us, it would save the country a great deal of expense and save a great deal of talk in this House and hard feelings, as well as those humiliating conversations between the hon. minister and his deputy.
You have a preliminary report of the- Transportation Commission ?
There is the report in respect to the St. John harbour.
No, I am leaving out the St. John harbour and the special report you brought down this evening. Have you a preliminary report besides these ?
Not that I am aware of.

Well, I am taking the answer of the right hon. Prime Minister :
Before the orders of the day are called, would the right hon. first minister tell us when we are to expect the preliminary report of the Transportation Committee.

Rideau canal extension, $50,000.
This is a revote of $50,000.
Is there any of it expended ?
Yes ; there was expended on surveys $566.66.
Are you going to take the weeds out of the Tay canal ?

No. There is a certain mill property belonging to certain parties- I forget the names, but I think they are Tott Brothers-for which a very large sum of money is claimed, and in order to build the locks at that place it will be nece'ssary
to have that property. The matter has not been gone on with. The surveys were not completed fully in time to go on last season, but in addition to that there is another difficulty arising in connection with this property.
This is for the purpose of establishing communication between the canal and a certain lake ?
Mud lake, Devil's lake and Desert lake.
Yes ; for the purpose of developing what was represented by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) as a large mining section.
Yes.

I hope the mines are there, that is all I can say.
Sault Ste. Marie canal-construction, $100,000.
Mr. SP-ROULE. What are you doing there ?

This is $100,000 we are asking for in addition to the $170,000 asked for last year. About $150,000 will he required to complete this work. The canal is cut through St. Mary's Island. It is 14 miles in length. The canal proper has a depth of 22 feet of water in the prism, with 24 feet 4 inches of water on the mitre sill of the lock. The deepening of the lower entrance to a depth of 21 feet 5 inches has been completed. The above amount is to be expended in removing shoals and deepening what is called the Vidal shoal and dredging and deepening the Upper Entrance so as to give a uniform depth of 21 feet 5 inches ; also to make a safer passage of vessels. There is, under contract, an extension of South Entrance Pier at lower entrance of canal of 800 feet. The substructure is of timber crib work with a superstructure of concrete ; at present there is only 18 feet in parts of upper entrance. Hinckler Bros, had a contract for deepening a portion of upper entrance at upper end of Vidal shoal. Their contract is completed. Tenders were advertised for; hut 011I3' one was received. Rate. 80 cents per yard. Tenders were called for in September, 1894, for deepening the upper entrance from eastern end of the entrance piers to the eastern end of what is known as the Vidal shoals. Five tenders were received. The work was awarded to the lowest tenderer-
0.	S. Boone, Toronto, at $1.74 per yard. No work has been done yet. Work is also under way in the extension of south entrance pier at lower entrance which will be finished next summer. Tenders were called for. Seven bids were received. The lowest tenderer, W. Birmingham, of Ottawa, was awarded the work at schedule rates. There was expended up to 30th November. 1904, $37,501.
When was the contract awarded to Mr. Birmingham ?

It was sometime after the vote of parliament. It was between that time and Christmas. A contract was also entered into with Messrs. O'Boyle Bros, for extending the south entrance pier, at the upper entrance of the canal. This is an extension of 800 feet and consists of a timber substructure capped with a concrete wall. This will make a safer entrance and avoid the cross current. Three tenders were received. The work was awarded to the lowest and amounts to $59,280.
What sum more will be required to complete the improvements V
About $150,000 more in addition to the $50,000 I spoke of.
